Stage 7: Repetition. Lally’s research reminds us that it takes on average about sixty-six days. So give yourself at least two or three months, coming back to the same practice again and again. There is no shortcut to spiritual maturity, only repetition.

Stage 8: Multiplication. When this practice has become your life, bring someone along to do it with you. Find your “2” and agree to ask each other one question every week: “This week, what is one thing you did in step with the Holy Spirit’s prompting?” That is where 235 relationships begin, and it is how God’s system is established.

Brothers and sisters, the eight stages are not eight steps you finish and then graduate from; they are a spiral, rising round after round. Each time you come back round to “Information”, you are standing on higher ground.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: May the Holy Spirit Navigate Your Whole Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, everything we have received today is built on the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Not one of the three can be missing.

Jesus gives us direction, the Bible gives us the standard, and the Holy Spirit is our navigator every day.

All of this is not just about passing on knowledge; it is about practice and revelation under the Holy Spirit’s leading. You could memorise the notes from the whole course and still live a life that relies on yourself; or you could remember just one sentence — “Holy Spirit, how do you see this?” — and from then on walk a completely different road.

When we are willing to let Jesus be King and let him receive the glory, the Holy Spirit will lead us step by step along the road he has prepared for us.

Come back to the picture we began with this morning. We are willing to hand an unfamiliar journey over to satellites we cannot see, yet unwilling to hand our whole life over to the Holy Spirit who lives within us. This morning, let’s put that order right.

Hand over the steering wheel. Not to fate, not to feelings, but to the true and living Counsellor who has been sent to our side.

May we practise every day: laying down our own cleverness, choosing to rely on the Holy Spirit’s leading, and walking a road that truly belongs to God.

May all the glory go to Jesus. He is King, and he is worthy.

“For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14)
“Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)
practices: Pray every day: “Holy Spirit, I am willing to be led by you today.”
Before deciding, pause and ask: “Holy Spirit, how do you see this?”
Each evening, quietly look back: did I obey the Holy Spirit today?
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.

Thank you that you not only sent your Son to die for us, but also sent your Holy Spirit to live within us. Thank you that you did not leave us to grope our way alone in the wilderness, but gave us the Counsellor to be our guide for life.

Lord, we confess that we have often treated you as an optional extra. We plan first and pray afterwards; we decide first and then ask you to bless it. By our own cleverness we have taken many needless detours and caused much needless hurt. Please forgive us.
Holy Spirit, I am willing to let you lead me today. Not relying on my plans, not relying on my cleverness, not relying on my experience. May you reign within me.
Make me willing to pause before every decision; let me hear you as I read your word; make me ever more sensitive to your promptings, and ever more watchful over my own voice.
Give me spiritual companions to steady me when I go my own way; and make me a companion to others, so that this road of relying on you is passed on.
May it no longer be we who live, but Christ who lives in us. May Jesus be King in our lives, and may all the glory go to him.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6) Think back over the last three months: what is one decision you made “without asking”? How did it turn out? If you could do it again, at what point would you stop first?

“For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14) Of the four channels of the Holy Spirit’s leading (God’s word, inner promptings and peace, circumstances and confirmation, the reminders and prayers of spiritual companions), which is most familiar to you? Which is least familiar? This week, in which channel are you willing to take a step?

blog.title: Who Is Navigating Your Life?

blocks.x: Subtitle: The Holy Spirit Is Not an Optional Extra but a Necessity
When you need to get somewhere you have never been, what do you do? You open your phone, type in the address and let the satnav lead the way.

That system depends on satellites in the sky. The baseline constellation of the Global Positioning System has at least twenty-four satellites orbiting some twenty thousand kilometres above the earth. You cannot see them, and you could not understand their signals, yet every day you trust them.
Here is the strange thing: we obey an invisible satellite system so readily, yet we are so often strangers to the true and living Holy Spirit who dwells within us.
He Is Not the Sunroof; He Is the Engine

We live in an age that leans on reason and prizes efficiency. We are used to analysing first, assessing first, and only at the very end do we think of praying. Sometimes prayer is no more than a “blessing on top”: the plan is already settled, and we simply ask God to bless the decision we have made ourselves. And so the Holy Spirit is quietly moved out to the edges of our faith, as though he were the sunroof on a new car — nice if you add it, but you can still drive without it.
But the Bible has never put the Holy Spirit in the options column.
“If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” (Galatians 5:25)

Listen to the logic of that sentence: if the beginning of your life was given by the Spirit, how can the walking out of your life rely on yourself? A life reborn by the Holy Spirit that goes about its days by the methods of the old self is like starting a car with the most advanced engine in the world and then getting out to push it along by hand.

The most powerful testimony of all comes from the Lord Jesus himself. At his baptism the Spirit came down on him; he was led by the Spirit into the wilderness; by the Spirit of God he cast out demons. He even said, “The Son can do nothing of himself.” (John 5:19)
If even Jesus relied on the Holy Spirit, who are we to dare to rely on ourselves?
The Key Is Not Technique but Attitude
We often ask: the Holy Spirit can’t be seen or touched — so how can I be led by him?
“Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

Notice that this passage does not teach us a method for discerning voices. It speaks of only three things: trust with all your heart, don’t lean on your own understanding, and acknowledge him in all your ways.

Many people strain desperately to “hear”, yet refuse first to “let go”. It is like turning the stereo up to full volume and then complaining that you can’t make out what someone is saying. The problem isn’t that the volume is too low; it’s that there’s too much noise — and the loudest noise inside us is our own voice.

Joshua chapter 9 records how the Gibeonites disguised themselves as envoys from a distant land and came to sue for peace, carrying mouldy bread. The leaders of Israel looked and touched, everything seemed to add up, and they made a covenant. Scripture pinpoints the whole problem in a single sentence: they didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh.
And so many of our mistakes today come not from being foolish but from not asking.
Three Practices, Starting Tomorrow Morning

First, each morning pray before you plan your schedule — just one sentence: “Holy Spirit, I am willing to be led by you today.” Most people reach for the phone the moment they open their eyes; our day is often crammed full of appointments before we have even met with God.
Second, before you decide, pause for one minute and ask: “Holy Spirit, how do you see this?” Most of life’s regrets happen in those minutes when we had no time to think.
Third, before bed each night, quietly ask three questions: Did I obey a prompting today? Did I ignore one? In what area tomorrow am I willing to be more sensitive?

The value of review has evidence behind it. In their 2014 research paper “Learning by Thinking”, Harvard Business School scholars including Francesca Gino, Gary Pisano and Bradley Staats found that people who spent about fifteen minutes a day writing down reflections went on to perform significantly better than a comparison group who spent the same time on extra practice.

It will certainly feel unfamiliar at first; that is perfectly normal. Research by Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London in 2010 found that forming a new habit takes on average about sixty-six days. If even brushing your teeth takes two months, how much more “ask the Holy Spirit first in everything”?
May the Holy Spirit Navigate Your Whole Life

The Three Foundations of Kingdom 321 are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Not one of the three can be missing. Jesus gives us direction, the Bible gives us the standard, and the Holy Spirit is our navigator every day. Without the Holy Spirit, the role model is just an impossibly high standard and the standard is just a strict set of rules; when the Holy Spirit comes, the role model becomes hope, and the standard becomes living water.

The core of the old self is self-centredness. A self-centred person will inevitably rely on himself, and whoever relies on himself will inevitably crowd out the Holy Spirit — for two kings cannot sit on the same throne at the same time. Relying on the Holy Spirit is selflessness at its most practical. And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless. A cup is emptied not so that it can stay empty, but so that it can be filled.
When we are willing to let Jesus be King and let him receive the glory, the Holy Spirit will lead us step by step along the road he has prepared for us.
Reflection Question
Looking back over the last three months, what decision did you make “without asking”? If you could do it again, at what point would you first stop and ask, “Holy Spirit, how do you see this?”

2. Picture: however good the air conditioner, if it isn’t plugged in it is just a very expensive metal box.
3. Quote Zechariah 4:6: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,” says Yahweh of Armies.
4. Scientific illustration: the Wiltschkos, Science, 1972 — the European robin navigates with a magnetic compass.

notes: Slide text:
Living by the Spirit Is the Mark of God’s Children

Key points:
1. Quote Romans 8:15: “You received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’”
2. “Abba” is Aramaic, the most intimate word a child in a Jewish home used for his father.
3. Old Testament prophecy: Ezekiel 36:27, “I will put my Spirit within you” — first the Spirit, then obedience.
4. Illustration: dozens of children in the street, but only one looks up, because it is his mother’s voice; knowing the voice comes through relationship.

notes: Slide text:

brief12.title: Key Point 3 (cont.)

1. Clarify: this is not abolishing reason. The Bereans were commended for “examining the Scriptures daily” (Acts 17:11).
2. The point is the order of surrender: not first analysing whether it’s feasible, but first seeking his will.
3. 321 saying: rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be sad; the outcomes of a whole life flow from the heart.

5. “Trust” is the Hebrew bāṭaḥ — to relax and hand over your whole weight.

brief21.title: Key Point 1 (1)
notes: Slide text:
The Holy Spirit Is Not an Optional Extra but a Necessity
“If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” (Galatians 5:25)
“Walk” in the original: to walk in line. If we live by the Spirit, how can we walk by ourselves?
Key points:
1. “Walk” is the Greek stoicheō — to walk in line, to advance in order; it is keeping in step, not strolling.
2. The spiritual life is not an improvised performance but an ongoing following, in step with the Spirit.
3. Picture: starting a car with the most advanced engine, then getting out and pushing it by hand.
4. Point out: we confess the Holy Spirit in the creeds, yet forget him at nine o’clock on Monday morning.

brief21.title: Key Point 1 (2)
notes: Slide text:
Even Jesus Did Not Act on His Own
“The Son can do nothing of himself.” (John 5:19)
“Apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)
Key points:
1. John 5:19 was spoken by the incarnate Son of God himself — it carries enormous weight.
2. John 15:5 has only two ends, “bears much fruit” and “can do nothing”; there is no third option.
3. In spiritual things there is no bare pass mark — only connected or cut off.
4. 321 application: the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances.

brief21.title: Key Point 1 (3)
notes: Slide text:
The Air Conditioner That Isn’t Plugged In
However good the machine, without power it is just a very expensive metal box.
“Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.” (Zechariah 4:6)
Key points:
1. Picture: the air conditioner isn’t broken; it simply isn’t connected — and so it is with many weary believers.
2. Zechariah 4:6 was spoken to Zerubbabel: facing ruins and opposition, what God gave first was not resources but a word.
3. Scientific illustration: the Wiltschkos, Science, 1972 — the European robin finds its bearings with a magnetic compass.
4. Application: if God has built a navigator into a small bird, how much more for the children he bought with his precious blood.
5. 321 application: the self-centred inevitably rely on themselves; relying on ourselves is everyday pride. Humility overcomes pride.

brief21.title: Key Point 2 (1)
notes: Slide text:
Being Led Is the Mark of God’s Children
“For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14)
Not “rather more spiritual”, but “the display of an identity”.
Key points:
1. Paul does not say those who are led are rather more spiritual; he says “these are children of God”.
2. Being led is a mark, not a rank; an identity, not an achievement.
3. Quote Romans 8:16: “The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God” — a double witness.
4. Illustration: growing quiet at a moment when you would normally lose your temper — in that moment the Spirit is setting his seal on you.

brief21.title: Key Point 2 (2)
notes: Slide text:
Not the Spirit of a Slave, but of a Child
“You received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15)
Abba: a child’s intimate word for father.
Key points:
1. “Abba” is Aramaic, the most intimate word a child in a Jewish home used for his father.
2. Paul deliberately set a household baby-word in his most rigorous theological letter.
3. Contrast: a slave listens for orders, a child for the father’s heart; a slave fears doing wrong, a child loves to be close.
4. Illustration: dozens of children in the street, but when his mother calls only one looks up — knowing the voice comes through relationship, not technique.

brief21.title: Key Point 2 (3)
notes: Slide text:
First the Spirit, Then Obedience
“I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes.” (Ezekiel 36:27)
321: first with God, then with people and things.
Key points:
1. Look at the order: first the Spirit is put within, then comes obedience — not obedience first, then the Spirit.
2. The Old Covenant law was written on stone; the New Covenant law is written on the heart, and the pen is the Holy Spirit.
3. Data: Iyengar and Lepper’s 2000 jam study — with twenty-four choices about 3% bought; with six, about 30%.
4. Application: what we lack is not options but a Guide.
5. 321 application: the order of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

brief21.title: Key Point 3 (1)
notes: Slide text:
Not Technique, but Attitude
“Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding, … he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)
Key points:
1. This passage teaches no technique for discerning voices; it speaks only of three attitudes.
2. “Acknowledge” is the Hebrew yādaʿ — recognising his sovereignty; “make straight” carries the sense of straightening, levelling.
3. Picture: the stereo on full volume, yet you can’t hear — the problem isn’t the volume but the noise; the loudest noise is ourselves.
4. The key is not whether we have heard, but whether we are willing to let go.

brief21.title: Key Point 3 (2)
notes: Slide text:
Rely on the heart, not the brain
Not abolishing reason, but letting the heart surrender before the head.
“Out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)
Key points:
1. Clarify: this is not abolishing reason. The Bereans were commended for “examining the Scriptures daily” (Acts 17:11).
2. The point is the order of surrender: seek his will first, then analyse feasibility.
3. The head is good at calculating risk, so when the head speaks first, fear is usually the loudest voice.
4. 321 saying: rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be sad; the outcomes of a whole life flow from the heart.

brief21.title: Key Point 3 (3)
notes: Slide text:
The Cost of Not Asking
“The men sampled their provisions, and didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh’s mouth.” Joshua 9:14
The Spirit forbade Paul to go to Asia — then came the Macedonian vision. Acts 16:6–10
Key points:
1. The Gibeonites’ trick: mouldy bread, split wineskins — everything added up, yet no one asked.
2. So many of our mistakes today come not from being foolish but from not asking.
3. Acts 16:6–7: it was a good plan — to preach the gospel — but the Holy Spirit said “no”.
4. The result: Paul turned to Troas, saw the Macedonian vision, and the gospel entered Europe for the first time.
5. Data: Lally’s team, 2010 — forming a new habit takes on average about sixty-six days (eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four).

brief21.title: Key Point 4 (1)
notes: Slide text:
Channel One: God’s Word
“Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” Psalm 119:105
A lamp to the feet lights the next step. The Spirit never leads against Scripture.
Key points:
1. Scripture is inspired by the Holy Spirit (2 Timothy 3:16); he knows best how to speak through the book he wrote.
2. An ancient lamp was a small hand-held oil lamp lighting only the next step — so read the Bible every day.
3. Hebrews 4:12: “The word of God is living and active … able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.”
4. Principle: any prompting that runs against the plain teaching of Scripture does not come from the Holy Spirit — without exception.
5. Application: morning devotion is not ticking off a reading plan but keeping a date with the Holy Spirit.

brief21.title: Key Point 4 (2)
notes: Slide text:
Channel Two: Promptings and Peace
“Let the peace of God rule in your hearts” (Colossians 3:15)
In the original: to act as umpire, to arbitrate. “Peace … which surpasses all understanding” Philippians 4:7
Key points:
1. “Rule” is the Greek brabeuō — to act as umpire, to arbitrate; when the heart argues back and forth, the referee blows the whistle.
2. Philippians 4:6–7: circumstances unchanged, difficulty not removed, yet the heart suddenly settled — “peace which surpasses all understanding”.
3. Discernment: agrees with Scripture, makes us humble, brings peace, stands the test of time, makes us love God and people more.
4. Scientific support: Dr Herbert Benson of Harvard Medical School, The Relaxation Response (1975) — stillness lowers heart rate and blood pressure.
5. Isaiah 30:15: “You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.”

brief21.title: Key Point 4 (3)
notes: Slide text:
Channels Three and Four: Circumstances and Companions
Align with the Lord first, then interpret. An open door doesn’t mean God wants you through it.
“It seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us” Acts 15:28 · “A threefold cord” Ecclesiastes 4:12
Key points:
1. Negative example: when Jonah wanted to flee to Tarshish, there just happened to be a ship in port (Jonah 1:3).
2. Isaiah 30:21: “Your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it.’” Often we obey first, and then see clearly.
3. Acts 13:2: as the church in Antioch served and fasted, the Spirit sent Barnabas and Saul — it happened in community.
4. Proverbs 27:6, “The wounds of a friend are faithful” — a companion is not a rubber stamp.
5. 321 application: the 235 relationships and the 920 practice bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23).

brief21.title: Practices (1)
notes: Slide text:
Practices (1)
Pray first thing each morning: “Holy Spirit, I am willing to be led by you today.”
Pause a minute before deciding: “Holy Spirit, how do you see this?”
Key points:
1. The key to Practice 1 is “first”: pray first, then plan your schedule.
2. Psalm 143:8: “Cause me to hear your loving kindness in the morning … Cause me to know the way in which I should walk.”
3. Practice 2: most of life’s regrets happen in the minute when we had no time to think.
4. James 1:19, “swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger”; James 1:5, God gives “without reproach”.

brief21.title: Practices (2)
notes: Slide text:
Practices (2)
Three bedtime questions: Did I obey? Did I ignore a prompting? Will I be more sensitive tomorrow?
The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Key points:
1. Three bedtime questions: Did I obey a prompting today? Did I ignore one? Where will I be more sensitive tomorrow?
2. Data: Gino, Pisano and Staats of Harvard Business School, in their 2014 research paper “Learning by Thinking”, found that
those who spent about fifteen minutes a day reflecting went on to perform significantly better than a comparison group who practised more.
3. Psalm 139:23–24: “Search me, God … and lead me in the everlasting way.”
4. Run through the eight stages one by one, stressing stage seven, Repetition, and stage eight, Multiplication.
5. Multiplication: find your “2” and ask each other one question every week — that is where 235 relationships begin.

brief21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
notes: Slide text:
The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
Three Foundations: role model, standard, guide. Two Core Values: King, all the glory.
The Goal: establish God’s system. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless.
Key points:
1. Without the Holy Spirit, the role model is only a high standard and the standard only strict rules; the Spirit turns knowledge into life.
2. Being led by the Spirit is the most everyday form of “let Jesus be King” — in this decision, who has the final say?
3. Galatians 2:20: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”
4. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless. A cup is emptied so that it can be filled.
5. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: Slide text:
May the Holy Spirit Navigate Your Whole Life
Jesus gives direction, the Bible gives the standard, the Holy Spirit is our daily navigator.
“He will glorify me.” (John 16:14) Let Jesus be King; all glory to him.
Key points:
1. Return to the Three Foundations and stress that not one of the three can be missing.
2. John 16:14, “He will glorify me” — the centre of the Spirit’s work is to glorify Jesus.
3. Any “leading” that makes people exalt themselves or gives the glory to people does not come from the Holy Spirit.
4. The call: return to the opening satnav picture and hand the steering wheel to the Counsellor today.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Prayer of Response and Blessing
Holy Spirit, I am willing to be led by you today. Not my plans, not my cleverness, not my experience.
May you reign within me. All glory to Jesus. Amen.
Key points:
1. Lead the congregation in praying aloud together a prayer of confession and surrender.
2. Pray for spiritual companions, asking the Lord to provide a “2” to support one another.
3. Blessing: may the Lord help us lay down our own cleverness daily and walk a road that truly belongs to God.
4. Preview the two small-group discussion questions and encourage the brothers and sisters to put this into practice this week.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today is Lesson 5 of Morning Devotion 321, the third of the Three Foundations — the Holy Spirit is my guide. We have already looked at Jesus is my role model and the Bible is my standard. Today we come to the one who “plugs in” the other two. Paul says, “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit” (Galatians 5:25). Brothers and sisters, listen to the logic of that sentence: if we receive life by the Spirit, how can we walk by our own strength?

Let me start with a question: who is navigating your life? When we need to get somewhere unfamiliar, we switch on the satnav on our phone. That system depends on at least twenty-four satellites in the sky; you can’t see them, yet every day you trust them. Isn’t it strange? We obey invisible satellites so readily, yet we are such strangers to the Holy Spirit who lives within us. In this age that prizes reason and efficiency, the Holy Spirit is often treated as an “optional extra” — nice to have, but you can still drive without him. But brothers and sisters, he is not the sunroof; he is the engine.

Our theme verse is Romans 8:14: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” Romans was written around AD 56 to 57. Chapter 7 is a person struggling under the law; then chapter 8 turns, and the whole chapter mentions the “Spirit” about twenty times. Paul is saying: the way to overcome the flesh is not to try harder, but to be led by the Spirit of God. Our other passage is Proverbs 3. The one who wrote “Don’t lean on your own understanding” was none other than Solomon, the wisest man in the Bible. Coming from his lips, those words carry exceptional weight.

Our first key point: the Holy Spirit is not an optional extra but a necessity. Even the Lord Jesus, while he was on earth, did not act on his own. At his baptism the Spirit came down on him; he was led by the Spirit into the wilderness; he cast out demons by the Spirit of God. He himself said, “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Brothers and sisters, if even Jesus relied on the Holy Spirit, who are we to dare to rely on ourselves? However good an air conditioner is, if it isn’t plugged in, it is just a very expensive metal box. Zechariah 4:6 says: not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit. Relying on ourselves is, in fact, pride at its most everyday.

Our second key point: living by the Spirit is the mark of God’s children. Paul doesn’t say, “As many as are led are rather more spiritual”; he says, “these are children of God.” The next verse is warmer still: you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage, but the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!” “Abba” is Aramaic, the most intimate word a little child uses for his father. A slave listens for orders; a child listens for the father’s heart. A slave is afraid of doing wrong; a child loves to be close. Brothers and sisters, dozens of children are running about in the street; the mother calls, and only one looks up — because it is his mother’s voice. Knowing the voice of the Holy Spirit comes not from technique but from relationship.

Our third key point: it is not about technique, but about attitude. We often ask: the Holy Spirit can’t be seen or touched — so how can I be led by him? Proverbs 3:5–6 gives the answer: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” See — it teaches no technique; it speaks only of attitude. The key is not whether we hear, but whether we are willing to let go. Joshua chapter 9 records a painful sentence: they didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh. Brothers and sisters, so many of our mistakes come not from being foolish, but from not asking.

Put simply: rely on the heart, not the brain. This is not abolishing reason; it is letting the heart surrender before the head does. Not first analysing whether it’s feasible, but first seeking his will. Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” Rely on the heart and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and you’ll be sad. It will feel unfamiliar at first — that’s perfectly normal. Research in 2010 by Lally’s team at University College London found that forming a new habit takes on average sixty-six days. If even brushing your teeth takes two months, how much more asking the Holy Spirit first in everything? So don’t give up.

Our fourth key point: the Holy Spirit leads us through four channels. First, through God’s word. Psalm 119:105 says, “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” Notice: a lamp to the feet — it lights the next step, not the next ten years. That’s why we need to read every day. There is one principle here: the Holy Spirit will never lead us to do anything that contradicts Scripture. Second, through inner promptings and peace. Colossians 3:15 tells us to let the peace of God rule in our hearts; that word originally means “to act as umpire”. When two roads lie before you, that referee will blow the whistle.

Third, through circumstances and confirmation. God uses people, events and things to confirm his leading, but the order must not be reversed: first align with the Lord, then interpret the circumstances. When Jonah wanted to flee to Tarshish, there just happened to be a ship in port. An open door does not necessarily mean God wants you to walk through it. Fourth, through the reminders and prayers of spiritual companions. The conclusion of the Council of Jerusalem is wonderful: “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us” — the Holy Spirit speaks through a group of people seeking together. This is exactly the 321 “235 relationships.” One person listening alone can easily mistake his own voice for God’s; a group of humble people listening together has protection.

Brothers and sisters, next come three practices. First, each morning, before you plan your schedule, pray one sentence: “Holy Spirit, I am willing to let you lead me today.” Second, before you make a decision, pause for one minute and ask: “Holy Spirit, how do you see this?” Most of life’s regrets happen in that one minute when we had no time to think. Third, before bed each night, quietly ask three questions: Did I obey a prompting today? Did I ignore a prompting? In what area tomorrow will I be more sensitive? Then walk it through the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Brothers and sisters, the whole 3-2-1 vision is built on the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Not one of the three can be missing. Jesus gives us direction, the Bible gives us the standard, and the Holy Spirit is our navigator every day. When the Lord spoke of the Holy Spirit, he made a point of saying, “He will glorify me.” So true leading never keeps the glory for people. When we are willing to let Jesus be King and let him receive the glory, the Holy Spirit will lead us step by step along the road he has prepared for us.

Let us pray together. Holy Spirit, I am willing to be led by you today. Not relying on my plans, not relying on my cleverness, not relying on my experience. Make me willing to pause before every decision, and make me ever more sensitive to your promptings. May it no longer be we who live, but Christ who lives in us. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, may we practise every day: laying down our own cleverness, choosing to rely on the Holy Spirit’s leading, and walking a road that truly belongs to God. May all the glory go to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today is Lesson 5 of Morning Devotion 321, the third of the Three Foundations — the Holy Spirit is my guide. We have already looked at Jesus is my role model and the Bible is my standard. Today’s foundation is the one that “plugs in” the other two. Paul says, “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit” (Galatians 5:25). Listen to the logic of that sentence: if the beginning of your life was given by the Spirit, how can the walking out of your life rely on yourself?

Let me start with a question: who is navigating your life? When we need to get somewhere unfamiliar, we open our phone and let the satnav lead the way. That system depends on satellites in the sky. The baseline constellation of the Global Positioning System has at least twenty-four satellites orbiting some twenty thousand kilometres above the earth; your phone has to pick up signals from at least four of them to work out where you are. You can’t see them, yet every day you trust them. Isn’t it strange? We obey invisible satellites so readily, yet we are such strangers to the Holy Spirit who lives within us. In this age that prizes reason and efficiency, the Holy Spirit is often treated as an “optional extra”. But brothers and sisters, he is not the sunroof; he is the engine.

The most powerful testimony of all comes from the Lord Jesus himself. At his baptism, “he saw the Spirit of God descending as a dove, and coming on him.” Before he began his ministry, he “was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.” In the synagogue, the first words out of his mouth were, “The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me.” When he cast out demons he said, “But if I by the Spirit of God cast out demons, then God’s Kingdom has come upon you.” Brothers and sisters, if even Jesus relied on the Holy Spirit, who are we to dare to rely on ourselves? The leading of the Holy Spirit is not a luxury, not the privilege of a spiritual elite; he is a daily necessity in the life of every Christian.

Our theme verse is Romans 8:14: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” Romans was written around AD 56 to 57, and it is the fullest statement of Paul’s theology. Chapter 7 is a person struggling under the law; then chapter 8 turns, and the whole chapter mentions the “Spirit” about twenty times — the most concentrated teaching on the Holy Spirit anywhere in the New Testament. Paul is saying: the way to overcome the flesh is not to try harder at keeping the law, but to be led by the Spirit of God. Our other passage is Proverbs 3 — the one who wrote “Don’t lean on your own understanding” was none other than Solomon, the wisest man in the Bible. Coming from his lips, those words carry exceptional weight.

Our first key point: the Holy Spirit is not an optional extra but a necessity. The word “walk” in Galatians 5:25 is the Greek stoicheō, which originally means “to walk in line”, like soldiers keeping step with the command, one stride at a time. Paul is not using the picture of a stroll; he is using the picture of keeping in step. Walking by the Spirit is not being moved now and then; it is keeping pace with the Holy Spirit day after day. Brothers and sisters, we confess the Holy Spirit in the creeds and sing his praise in our hymns; but in the office at nine o’clock on a Monday morning, how many times have we actually stopped and asked, “Holy Spirit, how do you see this?”

Look at how the Lord Jesus lived. John 5:19: “The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing.” The Son of God, the Word made flesh, stood on this earth and said: I can do nothing of myself. Then what about us? In John 15:5 the Lord says it even more directly: “Apart from me you can do nothing.” Notice the two ends of that sentence: at one end is bearing much fruit, at the other is being able to do nothing, and there is no third option in between. In spiritual things there is no bare pass mark — only connected or cut off.

I often think of the air conditioner at home. However fine an air conditioner is, however well designed, if it isn’t plugged in, it is just a very expensive metal box. It isn’t broken; it simply isn’t connected to the power. That is the condition of many Christians: not that they aren’t earnest enough, but that they aren’t plugged in. We use our own willpower to love the person who is so hard to love, and the result is exhaustion. Zechariah 4:6 says, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.” The natural world bears witness too: the Wiltschkos published in Science in 1972 that the European robin finds its bearings with a magnetic compass. If God has built a navigator even into a small bird, would he leave his children to lose their way in the wilderness?

Our second key point: being led is the mark of God’s children. Paul doesn’t say, “Those who are led are rather more spiritual”; he says, “these are children of God.” Being led is a mark, not a rank; an identity, not an achievement. Verse 16 of the same chapter says, “The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God.” It is a double witness. Brothers and sisters, when, in a moment where you would normally lose your temper, you suddenly grow quiet; when, at a moment where you could take advantage, you choose to take the loss — in that moment the Holy Spirit is setting his seal upon you.

The next verse is warmer still. Romans 8:15: “For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” “Abba” is Aramaic, the most intimate word a little child in a Jewish home would use for his father. Paul took that household baby-word and set it in the most rigorous theological letter he ever wrote. A slave listens for orders; a child listens for the father’s heart. A slave is afraid of doing wrong; a child loves to be close. Brothers and sisters, it is getting dark, and a mother calls her child’s name from the front door; dozens of children are running about in the street, but only one lifts his head — because it is his mother’s voice. Knowing the voice of the Holy Spirit is just the same: it comes not from technique but from relationship.

Ezekiel 36:27 says, “I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes.” Look at the order: first the Spirit is put within, and only then comes obedience. It is not that you obey God first and then he gives you his Spirit; God gives you his Spirit first, and only then are you able to obey. Psychology offers supporting evidence too: in their 2000 jam study, Iyengar of Columbia University and Lepper of Stanford found that the display with twenty-four jams had a purchase rate of only about three per cent, while the display with just six reached about thirty per cent. With too many choices, people simply freeze. What we lack is not options but a Guide.

Our third key point is the question everyone most wants to ask: the Holy Spirit can’t be seen or touched — so how can I be led by him? Proverbs 3:5–6 gives the answer: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” It is not about technique but about attitude. “Trust” in Hebrew is bāṭaḥ, which means to lean back and rest on — like a child flopping, whole body, into his father’s arms. Brothers and sisters, many people strain desperately to “hear”, yet refuse first to “let go”. It is like turning the stereo up to full volume and then complaining that you can’t make out what someone is saying. The problem isn’t the volume; it’s the noise — and the loudest noise is our own voice.

Put simply: rely on the heart, not the brain. This is not abolishing reason. The Bereans were “examining the Scriptures daily”, and Scripture commends them for it. When 321 says “rely on the heart and not the brain”, it means an order of surrender: let the heart surrender before the head does. Not first analysing whether it’s feasible, but first seeking his will. Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” Rely on the heart and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and you’ll be sad. Why? Because the head is good at calculating risk, and when the head speaks first, fear is usually the loudest voice.

Joshua chapter 9 gives us a painful example. The Gibeonites disguised themselves as envoys from a distant land and came to sue for peace, carrying mouldy bread and split wineskins. The leaders of Israel looked and touched, everything seemed to add up, and they made a covenant. Scripture pinpoints the whole problem in a single sentence: they didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh. Brothers and sisters, it wasn’t that they weren’t clever enough; it was that they didn’t ask. By contrast, Acts 16 records that Paul wanted to preach in Asia, but the Holy Spirit forbade him; he tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit didn’t allow him. It was a good plan — they were going to preach the gospel — but the Holy Spirit said “no”. So Paul changed course, saw the vision of the man from Macedonia, and the gospel set foot in Europe for the first time. Sometimes the Holy Spirit’s “no” is more precious than his “yes”.

Our fourth key point: the Holy Spirit leads us through four channels. First, through God’s word. Scripture is inspired by the Holy Spirit, so of course he knows best how to use the book he wrote to speak to us. Psalm 119:105 says, “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” An ancient lamp was a small oil lamp carried in the hand, and it lit about one step ahead. God’s word is mostly not a searchlight that lights up the next ten years of your future in one sweep; it is a lamp to your feet. That’s why we need to read the Bible every day — the lamp has to stay in our hand for the path to stay lit. There is one principle here: the Holy Spirit will never lead us to do anything that contradicts Scripture.

Second, through inner promptings and peace. Colossians 3:15 says, “And let the peace of God rule in your hearts.” “Rule” in Greek is brabeuō, which originally means “to act as umpire”. When two roads lie before you and your heart argues back and forth without end, that referee will blow the whistle. Philippians 4:7 says, “And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” The circumstances haven’t changed, the difficulty hasn’t been removed, and yet you suddenly find yourself settled — that peace is not something you manufacture; it is something he gives. We must also be honest: feelings can deceive, so this channel must always be used together with the first. A true prompting agrees with Scripture, makes us humble, and stands the test of time.

Third, through circumstances and confirmation. God really does arrange circumstances, but circumstances are not a self-translating dictionary. When Jonah wanted to flee to Tarshish, there just happened to be a ship in port bound for Tarshish. Brothers and sisters, an open door does not necessarily mean God wants you to walk through it. The order must not be reversed: first align with God’s will, then use circumstances as confirmation. Isaiah 30:21 says, “Your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it.’” Sometimes you have to take a step forward before you will hear it. Fourth, through spiritual companions. The conclusion of the Council of Jerusalem says, “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us.” The Holy Spirit speaks through a group of people seeking together. This is exactly the 321 “235 relationships” — a group of humble people listening together has protection.

Next come three practices. Practice 1: when you get up each morning, before you plan your schedule, pray one sentence: “Holy Spirit, I am willing to let you lead me today; I won’t rely on my own plans — may you reign.” Notice the word “before”. Most people reach for the phone the moment they open their eyes; our day is often crammed full of appointments before we have even met with God. Practice 2: before you decide, stop for a moment, keep your mouth shut for one minute, and ask: “Holy Spirit, how do you see this?” Brothers and sisters, most of life’s regrets happen in those minutes when we had no time to think. James tells us that God “gives to all liberally and without reproach” — he won’t find you a nuisance for coming to ask again.

Practice 3: before bed each night, quietly ask three questions. Was there one thing today that I did in obedience to the Holy Spirit’s prompting? Was there a prompting today that I ignored? In what area tomorrow am I willing to be more sensitive? The value of review has evidence behind it: in their 2014 research paper “Learning by Thinking”, Harvard Business School scholars including Gino, Pisano and Staats found that people who spent about fifteen minutes a day writing down reflections went on to perform significantly better than a comparison group who spent the same time on extra practice. Then walk it through the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Lally’s 2010 research says forming a new habit takes on average about sixty-six days, so please give yourself two or three months.

Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s message back into the picture of 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Without the Holy Spirit, the role model is just an impossibly high standard, and the standard is just a strict set of rules. When the Holy Spirit comes, the role model becomes hope, and the standard becomes living water. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory — being led by the Holy Spirit is the most everyday form of “letting Jesus be King”. The Goal: establish God’s system. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Galatians 2:20 says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless.

Brothers and sisters, everything we have received today is built on the Three Foundations, and not one of the three can be missing. Jesus gives us direction, the Bible gives us the standard, and the Holy Spirit is our navigator every day. When the Lord spoke of the Holy Spirit, he made a point of saying, “He will glorify me.” So true leading never keeps the glory for people. Come back to the picture we began with this morning: we are willing to hand an unfamiliar journey over to satellites we cannot see, yet unwilling to hand our whole life over to the Holy Spirit who lives within us. This morning, let’s put that order right. Hand over the steering wheel — not to fate, not to feelings, but to the true and living Counsellor.

Let us pray together. Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that you not only sent your Son to die for us, but also sent your Holy Spirit to live within us. Lord, we confess that we have often treated you as an optional extra — we plan first and pray afterwards; we decide first and then ask you to bless it. Please forgive us. Holy Spirit, I am willing to be led by you today. Not relying on my plans, not relying on my cleverness, not relying on my experience. Make me willing to pause before every decision, and make me ever more sensitive to your promptings. Give me spiritual companions. May it no longer be we who live, but Christ who lives in us. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

Brothers and sisters, may we practise every day: laying down our own cleverness, choosing to rely on the Holy Spirit’s leading, and walking a road that truly belongs to God. May Jesus be King, and may all the glory go to him.

sections.heading: Introduction: Whose Hands Are on the Wheel?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Please picture a scene with me first.

A husband and wife set out in the car. He is driving; she is in the passenger seat. The junction ahead is jammed, and she says, “You should have taken that side street back there.” He says nothing and turns the music up a little. Two junctions later she says, “See? I told you so.” He turns the music up a little more. A bit further on, the satnav says, “Make a U-turn ahead,” and she reaches across and gives the steering wheel a nudge to the right.

The car doesn’t overturn, but for the rest of that day the two of them don’t say another word to each other.

Brothers and sisters, a car can only have one steering wheel. When the hand from the passenger seat reaches across, it isn’t helping; it’s grabbing. We all laugh at this scene, because we are all in it. That hand is in our marriages, that hand is in our workplaces, that hand is in our church service, and that hand is in our prayers too — even as we say, “Lord, your will be done,” we quietly nudge the wheel towards the direction we want.

Today we enter the second part of Kingdom 321. In the last five lessons we looked together at the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. With the foundations laid, next come the Two Core Values. The first of these core values is today’s theme — let Jesus be King.

“Let Jesus be King” is not a slogan, not the chorus of a worship song, not a rousing line we shout at the end of a meeting. It is the centre of the whole system of our faith. It is a decision — a decision that has to be made afresh every morning: today, whose hands are on the wheel?

Let me begin with something that may sting a little: a person can love Jesus very much, serve Jesus very zealously, and yet never have let Jesus be King. Because loving him and serving him can still mean “I am King, and he is helping me.” Letting Jesus be King is the opposite order — he is King, and I am following.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The King and the Kingdom in the Sermon on the Mount
sections.html:
Our key passage comes from Matthew chapter 7.

The author of Matthew’s Gospel is the apostle Matthew, formerly a tax collector in Capernaum, who was called by the Lord to become one of the twelve apostles. Most evangelical scholars hold that this Gospel was written somewhere between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for communities of Jewish believers. That is why Matthew opens his very first verse with: “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1). “Son of David” is a royal title. From beginning to end, Matthew sets out to prove one thing: this Jesus of Nazareth is the King the Jewish people had been waiting for through hundreds of years.

That is why the phrase “Kingdom of Heaven” appears more than thirty times in Matthew. The first thing the wise men from the east asked when they arrived was, “Where is he who is born King of the Jews?” (Matthew 2:2). The first message the Lord Jesus preached when he began his ministry was, “Repent! For the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand” (Matthew 4:17). When he was crucified, the sign on the cross read, “THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS” (Matthew 27:37). And the first thing he said to his disciples after his resurrection was, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28:18).

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The whole of Matthew’s Gospel is the record of a coronation.

And the Sermon on the Mount, in chapters 5 to 7, is the charter of the kingdom proclaimed by this King. He is not teaching a somewhat higher grade of morality; he is declaring: in my kingdom, this is how things work. So he says blessed are the poor in spirit, he says love your enemies, he says don’t be anxious about tomorrow, he says seek first his Kingdom and his righteousness. If these words did not come from the mouth of a true King, they would all be empty words.

Chapter 7 is the conclusion, and the Lord Jesus sums up with four contrasts in a row: two roads, two kinds of tree, two kinds of people, two foundations. Our key verse falls in the third — two kinds of people.

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 7:21)

Notice the title “Lord”. In Greek it is κύριε (kyrie), from κύριος (kyrios), meaning master, owner, the one with absolute right to dispose of what is his. In the Roman world it was what a slave called his master, and what a subject called Caesar. When someone calls Jesus “Lord”, the very grammar of it already concedes: all that I have is his, and he may dispose of it entirely as he wishes.

The Lord Jesus says: saying it is not enough.

Luke’s Gospel records the same teaching in even more direct terms: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say?” (Luke 6:46). The Lord Jesus is exposing a spiritual contradiction: with our lips we set him on the throne, while in our living we ask him to step down from it.

That is the question we must face today.

sections.heading: 1. Only Jesus Is Worthy to Be King
sections.html:
The lesson begins by setting the most important reason right in front of us: because only Jesus died for our sins, only he rose from the dead and overcame the power of Satan and of Hades, he alone is worthy to reign and to sit upon the throne.

That word “worthy” is the bedrock of this lesson.

Revelation chapter 5 shows us the most solemn scene in heaven. In God’s right hand is a scroll, sealed tight with seven seals. A mighty angel proclaims with a loud voice, “Who is worthy to open the book, and to break its seals?” (Revelation 5:2). And no one in heaven, on earth or under the earth was worthy to open the scroll or to look into it. So John wept bitterly. Then one of the elders said to him, “Don’t weep. Behold, the Lion who is of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has overcome: he who opens the book and its seven seals” (Revelation 5:5).

The word “worthy” is the Greek ἄξιος (axios). It was originally a word from trade and measurement, meaning “of equal weight” — placed on one side of the scales, it exactly balances what is on the other side, no more and no less. So “worthy” is not a polite compliment, and not a matter of our voting for him; it is a fact that has been weighed: only his weight matches that throne.

So on what grounds is he worthy? The Bible gives three answers.

First, because he died for our sins.

The new song in heaven goes like this: “You are worthy to take the book and to open its seals: for you were killed, and bought us for God with your blood out of every tribe, language, people, and nation” (Revelation 5:9). Notice that word “for”. The reason he is worthy is not his almighty power — he was almighty all along; the reason is “you were killed”. In heaven, the one on the throne does not appear in the form of a lion; what John saw was “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6).

Brothers and sisters, what a wonderful thing this is. Every throne in this world was won with other people’s blood; only this one throne was won with the King’s own blood.

Second, because he rose from the dead and overcame the power of Satan and of Hades.

“who was declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:4). The resurrection is God’s most public coronation of this King.

Paul describes it more concretely: “Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (Colossians 2:15). Hebrews puts it in words that come even closer to our hearts: “Since then the children have shared in flesh and blood, he also himself in the same way partook of the same, that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and might deliver all of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage” (Hebrews 2:14–15).

Third, because God the Father has exalted him to the highest place.

“Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Philippians 2:9–11)

“He has on his garment and on his thigh a name written, ‘KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS.’” (Revelation 19:16)

So letting Jesus be King is not us doing him a favour, not us generously giving up our seat for him. He has always been on the throne. What we call “letting” is really acknowledging the facts — coming back to the truth.

Let me use an illustration. While the grown-ups are out, a little boy climbs into his father’s office chair, picks up the company seal and stamps away happily. He’s having a wonderful time, and he feels very important. But that chair has never for one second belonged to him. When his father comes in and he climbs down from the chair, he hasn’t “lost” anything; he has gone back to where he belongs — back to the place of a son, which is a better place than the boss’s.

Brothers and sisters, letting Jesus be King means climbing down from a chair that was never ours.

In 1880, in his address at the founding of the Free University of Amsterdam, the Dutch theologian and statesman Abraham Kuyper said words that are still quoted today: there is not a square inch in the whole domain of our human existence over which Christ, who is sovereign over all, does not cry, “Mine!”

Not a square inch. Not ninety per cent, not the two hours on Sunday — every square inch.

Seen through 321, this is the first of the Two Core Values. The Three Foundations are the root: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. When the root is firmly planted, it must bear the fruit of the core values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. And the purpose of it all is to establish God’s system.

Brothers and sisters, remember this order: first we see that he is worthy; only then are we glad to let him be King. If we don’t first see that he is worthy, “let Jesus be King” turns into a religious burden instead of a response of love.

sections.heading: 2. Everyone Is Born Wanting to Be King
sections.html:
The lesson says: every one of us is born wanting to “be king ourselves” — wanting to control our lives, call the shots, even manipulate others. And it is precisely this “I’ll be king” attitude that becomes the root of every quarrel, every confusion and everything that destroys unity.

The Bible’s very first tragedy was a struggle for the throne. The serpent said to the woman, “For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). “Like God” — that was the first advertising slogan in human history, and the most successful one ever. What it was selling was not fruit; it was a throne.

This temptation appeared even earlier, in the fall of the angels. Isaiah records the monologue: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14). In just two verses, five times: “I will”.

Brothers and sisters, the grammar of pride is the first person.

321 says: “self” is the root of our fall; pride is the root of the problem. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights that are not ours, wanting to take God’s place. What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

The book of Judges sums up the chaos of a whole era in a single sentence: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25). Notice the cause and effect between those two sentences: because there was no king, everyone did what was right in his own eyes. If a family has no king, everyone does as they please; if a church has no king, everyone does as they please too. The chaos isn’t because people are so very wicked; the chaos is because the throne is empty.

Later, when the Israelites demanded a king, God said to Samuel: “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me as the king over them” (1 Samuel 8:7). It wasn’t that they didn’t want a king; they didn’t want this King. They wanted a king they could see, who would listen to them and do things their way.

In the New Testament, the Lord Jesus says in a parable: “But his citizens hated him, and sent an envoy after him, saying, ‘We don’t want this man to reign over us’” (Luke 19:14).

From Eden to the cross, humanity’s problem has always been the same sentence: we don’t want this man to reign over us.

Here I want to mention a psychological study that helps us see ourselves. In 1975 the psychologist Ellen Langer published a famous paper in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology entitled “The Illusion of Control”. She ran a series of experiments, one of which went like this: two groups of people bought identical lottery tickets; one group could choose their own numbers, while the other group were handed tickets at random. The odds of winning were exactly the same. But when the researchers later tried to buy the tickets back, the group who had picked their own numbers asked for a markedly higher price.

Langer named this phenomenon “the illusion of control” — people systematically overestimate how much control they have over outcomes.

Brothers and sisters, this study says nothing about faith, yet it describes our condition precisely. We grip the steering wheel tightly not because we can really control things, but because holding on to something makes us feel secure inside. What we are clutching is often nothing more than a lottery ticket whose odds haven’t changed at all.

That is why the Lord Jesus spoke our key verse: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 7:21).

Brothers and sisters, the title is a matter for the mouth; doing his will is a matter of kingship. I can call him Lord in the most devout tone of voice and at the same time be king myself in every decision. What the Lord Jesus looks at is not our volume but our steering wheel.

Then he says, “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock” (Matthew 7:24). He didn’t say, “Everyone who hears these words of mine and is moved”; he said, “and does them”.

321’s fivefold change says it clearly: change of mindset, change of life, change of daily living, change of relationships, change of ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. A faith that stops at the “title” has stopped at the Information stage and has not yet entered into life. Today’s lesson wants to take us one step further: from a title on our lips to a handing-back in our daily living.

sections.heading: 3. Wherever Jesus Is King, There Is Victory
sections.html:
The lesson says: Jesus is the victorious King; he has already overcome every power of darkness. When we are willing to let Jesus be King in every area of our lives, that area will experience victory.

The reverse is also true: wherever we don’t let Jesus be King, we go on losing battles.

It isn’t that God refuses to help us; it’s that we haven’t invited the King in. If the city gates aren’t opened, the King’s army won’t force its way in. The psalm cries out: “Lift up your heads, you gates! Be lifted up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory will come in” (Psalm 24:7).

(1) Let Jesus Be King over Our Emotions

The lesson says: if we let Jesus be King over our emotions, we will no longer be ruled by anger, fear and anxiety.

The Bible saw long ago that emotions are a battlefield: “One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city” (Proverbs 16:32). And again: “Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint” (Proverbs 25:28).

For an ancient city, its walls were its life. Once the walls were breached, no enemy army needed to attack — anyone could just walk in. Brothers and sisters, a person whose emotions have no King over them is a city without walls — a colleague’s remark can walk in, a family member’s expression can walk in, a comment online can walk in, and once inside it settles down in your heart and stays for days.

Paul says, “‘Be angry, and don’t sin.’ Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath, and don’t give place to the devil” (Ephesians 4:26–27). Notice the words “give place”. Nursing anger until sunset is setting aside a plot of ground in your heart for the enemy to build a house on.

There is a fascinating finding from psychology here. In 2007 a team led by the psychologist Matthew Lieberman at the University of California, Los Angeles, published a study in the journal Psychological Science. They showed participants pictures of disturbing faces while observing their brains with functional magnetic resonance imaging. They found that when participants simply “felt” the emotion, the amygdala was highly active; but when they put the emotion into words and labelled it — for example, “this is anger”, “this is fear” — activity in the amygdala dropped markedly, and the regulating regions of the prefrontal cortex became active. The researchers call this phenomenon “affect labelling”.

Brothers and sisters, hear me clearly: this study cannot save us; only Scripture can save us. But from one angle it confirms a spiritual fact — bring an emotion into the light, say it out loud, hand it over, and the emotion loses its violence.

And Christians have something better than naming, and it’s called prayer: “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:6–7). The Greek verb for “guard”, φρουρέω (phroureō), is a military term meaning to post soldiers to garrison the city gates. When you hand over your anxiety, the King sends his peace to stand sentry.

321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be sad, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad. Out of the heart flows the wellspring of life (see Proverbs 4:23). Emotions are not managed by suppression; they are governed by a change of King.

(2) Let Jesus Be King in Our Families

The lesson says: if we let Jesus be King in our families, our families can experience reconciliation and healing.

When Joshua was old, he gathered all the people at Shechem and said to them, “As for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh” (Joshua 24:15). Notice that he didn’t say, “As for me”; he said, “me and my house”. A family needs someone to stand up first and decide, on the family’s behalf, who the King is.

Brothers and sisters, nine times out of ten, quarrels at home are not about right and wrong; they are about the throne. Who has the final say? Who has to apologise? Who backs down first? As long as there are two kings under one roof, the home is a battlefield. 321 puts it exactly: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Paul’s prescription is simple, yet hard: “bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do” (Colossians 3:13).

The psychologist John Gottman of the University of Washington in the United States has studied marital interaction for many years. He identified four patterns of communication that do the most damage to a relationship and called them “the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse”: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that every one of these four is an expression of “I want to be king”? Criticism is me sitting in the judge’s seat; contempt is me placing myself above the other person; defensiveness is me guarding my borders to the death; stonewalling is me declaring by my silence: on this, my word is final.

If there is a King in the home, these four horsemen cannot get in. Because once the King is seated on the throne, I have stepped down from the judge’s seat.

(3) Let Jesus Be King over Our Money

The lesson says: if we let Jesus be King over our money, we will be set free from greed and enter into trust and abundance.

When the Lord Jesus spoke about money, he used the language of kingship: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24).

He didn’t say “you shouldn’t”; he said “you can’t”. This is a statement about what is possible, not a piece of moral advice. Money is not a neutral tool; money will try to be king. The Lord Jesus personifies it and calls it “Mammon”.

The Lord Jesus also said, “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21). Brothers and sisters, you can use that sentence as a mirror. Do you want to know where your heart is? Look at your bank statements. Do you want to know who you’ve given the throne to? Look at the sum you would find hardest to part with.

In 2008 Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton published a study in the journal Science. They gave participants a sum of money and randomly assigned one group to spend it on themselves and the other to spend it on others. When their happiness was measured that evening, the group who had spent the money on others were noticeably happier.

The Lord Jesus said this long ago: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

Seeking God’s kingdom first is not a financial strategy; it is the order of kingship: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well” (Matthew 6:33). In Malachi, God even makes an exceptional invitation to put him to the test: “Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house, and test me now in this,” says Yahweh of Armies, “if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there will not be room enough for” (Malachi 3:10).

321’s shift of perspective is at its most practical here: from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal. The money is the same money, but when the King is on the throne, money goes from being master to being servant.

(4) Let Jesus Be King in Our Relationships

The lesson says: if we let Jesus be King in our relationships, conflicts can be resolved and we can be one with each other.

In his high-priestly prayer before his suffering, this is what the Lord Jesus asked for us: “that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me” (John 17:21).

Paul says, “being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3). “Eager to keep” means that unity does not happen by itself; unity has to be guarded.

Brothers and sisters, why won’t a conflict resolve? Because at the scene of a conflict there are usually two kings, and no King. When two kings are present, all you can do is decide a winner and a loser; only when one King is present can there be reconciliation.

Picture an orchestra. Twenty-odd people, each with a different instrument in hand, each with a different part on the music stand. Without a conductor, each would play to his own beat, and the harder they tried, the worse the noise. But the moment the conductor raises the baton, the very same twenty-odd people with the very same different parts become a symphony. The conductor hasn’t replaced anyone; he has simply given them one beat.

Jesus being King is that baton. Unity has never meant making everyone the same; unity means everyone looking to the same King.

321’s 920 practice says: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”. As we practise living a selfless (0) life, the nine (9) graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow in these relationships — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, fruit is not something we manufacture; fruit is the result of the King’s reign. Whichever relationship lets Jesus be King is the relationship that begins to bear fruit.

The lesson sums up this section in one sentence that I love: whichever part of our life hands over its sovereignty will move from chaos into order, from a breach into blessing.

sections.heading: 4. Letting Jesus Be King Means Handing Back Sovereignty
sections.html:
The lesson says: at the moment we came to faith, we said, “I receive Jesus as my Saviour and the Lord of my life.” That was not just the beginning of faith; it was a transfer of sovereignty — I no longer live for myself, but let Jesus be Lord and reign in my life.

In history, when a city changed hands, there was a ceremony of handover: the old governor of the city would lay the keys of the city gates on a tray and present them with both hands to the new king. From that moment on, the city’s taxes, laws, defences and comings and goings all came under the new king. When the keys were handed over, it wasn’t a piece of iron that changed hands; it was a whole city.

Paul turns this into the most personal of testimonies: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

This is what 321 means: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Selflessness is not having nothing, not wiping ourselves out; selflessness is no longer being confined by that small “self”, but entering into the limitless and living out the limitless. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

The lesson lists four areas in which sovereignty must be handed back. Let’s look at them one by one.

(1) Personal Life: No Longer Deciding Life’s Direction by Ourselves

The lesson says: no longer deciding the direction of our lives by ourselves, but seeking God’s will and obeying his leading.

In the Garden of Gethsemane the Lord Jesus himself set the example for us: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42).

Notice the structure of this verse. The first half is honesty: he does not pretend it doesn’t hurt. The second half is handing back: nevertheless, not my will. Brothers and sisters, handing back sovereignty doesn’t mean feeling nothing; it means feeling everything and still saying “nevertheless”.

Every day we meet that “nevertheless”. A child’s ambitions, whether to stay in a job or leave, a health report, a relationship we have waited on for a long time without any answer. We can all say the first half; the second half takes grace.

Paul urges us like this: “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service” (Romans 12:1). The sacrifices of the Old Testament were dead; the sacrifice of the New Testament is living. The biggest problem with a living sacrifice is that it keeps crawling off the altar. So handing back sovereignty is not a one-off ceremony; it is a decision, every morning, to climb back onto the altar.

321 says: the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. If the direction of our life is not first set true with God, every decision that follows will drift.

(2) Relationships: No Longer Reacting from Our Emotions

The lesson says: no longer reacting from our emotions, but letting Jesus be King in our relationships and living out forgiveness, forbearance and unity.

“Reacting” and “responding” sound almost alike, yet a whole throne lies between them. Reacting is when someone presses my button and I leap up — the button is in their hand, which means the throne is in their hand. Responding is when I first bring the matter before the King, and then decide how to speak.

Peter says, “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (1 Peter 5:5). The word behind “clothe yourselves” pictures tying on an apron — what a servant does before starting work, the very thing the Lord Jesus did at the Last Supper when he took a towel, tied it around himself and washed the disciples’ feet (see John 13:4–5).

Brothers and sisters, humility is not thinking badly of yourself; humility is returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Only when I no longer need to win every conversation am I truly free.

(3) Resources and Finances: No Longer Storing Up Wealth Just for Ourselves

The lesson says: no longer storing up wealth just for ourselves, but letting Jesus direct how our money is used, to the glory of his kingdom.

The Lord Jesus told a parable about a rich man. His land produced a bumper harvest, so he planned to pull down his barns and build bigger ones. There is a jarring detail in what he says: “What will I do, because I don’t have room to store my crops? … This is what I will do. I will pull down my barns, build bigger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods” (Luke 12:17–18). In just two verses, “I” five times and “my” four times — and the next verse has still more. But God said to him: “You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared — whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20).

Brothers and sisters, this rich man was not a villain; he was simply his own king. And the end of being your own king is that not one of his plans had God written into it, and not one had other people written into it.

As David prepared the offerings for the temple, he prayed: “I know also, my God, that you try the heart, and have pleasure in uprightness. As for me, in the uprightness of my heart I have willingly offered all these things” (1 Chronicles 29:17). And he said: “For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own” (1 Chronicles 29:14).

That is handing back sovereignty in our finances: I am not giving to God; I am giving back to God.

(4) Choices of Time: No Longer Arranging Everything for Ourselves

The lesson says: no longer arranging everything for ourselves, but being willing to set time apart for the Lord, seeking first his kingdom and his righteousness.
