Ask: if we, by grace, are used by God but then exalt ourselves, could we fall into the same danger?
Reminder: stealing glory is no small thing; it is a grave spiritual offence.

brief21.title: 3c. A Darkened Mind
notes: They didn’t glorify him as God or give thanks
Vain in reasoning, their heart darkened
Romans 1:21
Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan
Key points:
The chain in Romans 1:21: failing to glorify and thank God is the cause; vain reasoning and a darkened heart are the effect.
The first punishment for stealing glory is a mind that begins to grow muddled.
Psychology: Jennifer Crocker and Lora Park, 2004, Psychological Bulletin, “The Costly Pursuit of Self-Esteem” — building self-worth on outside approval costs us over the long run.
Luke 10:20: if even authority over demons is not worth rejoicing in, how much less the applause of people.
321 application: humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan; Satan finds no foothold in someone who has emptied out the self.

brief21.title: 4. Earth Is Temporary, Heaven Eternal
notes: They have received their reward
A commercial term: paid in full
Collect it all on earth, nothing left in heaven
Key points:
Matthew 6:2 on giving, 6:5 on prayer, 6:16 on fasting: the same conclusion three times.
The original ἀπέχω is a commercial term meaning “paid in full” — like stamping “PAID.”
John 12:42–43: rulers believed in their hearts but didn’t confess it, because they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise.
Reminder: collect all the glory on earth and we cannot receive the true reward in heaven.

brief21.title: 4b. Fireworks and Starlight
notes: Earthly glory: fireworks, three seconds
Shine as the stars for ever and ever
Daniel 12:3
From a temporary perspective to an eternal one
Key points:
Illustration: fireworks are gone in three seconds, leaving a wisp of smoke and paper on the ground.
Daniel 12:3: they will shine as the stars for ever and ever.

Example: the eighteenth-century missionary movement of the Moravian Brethren under Count Zinzendorf (1700–1760); their watchword is generally said to have been “May the Lamb that was slain receive the reward of his suffering.”
321 application: a shift in perspective — from man’s to God’s, earthly to heavenly, temporary to eternal, worldly to godly.
Ask: do you want to be a three-second firework, or a star for ever and ever?

brief21.title: 5. Selflessness: Let the Self Step Down
notes: I have been crucified with Christ
It is no longer I who live
But Christ lives in me
Galatians 2:20
Key points:
Galatians 2:20: selflessness is letting the self step down.
321 emphasis: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living it out.
Illustration: a cup full of itself has no room for anything else; emptied, it gives God room to fill it.
Philippians 2:6–8: Christ emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.

brief21.title: 5b. Hiddenness: Willing to Be Unseen
notes: Your life is hidden with Christ in God
Colossians 3:3
He must increase, but I must decrease
John 3:30
Key points:
Colossians 3:3: our life is hidden with Christ in God.
The model of John the Baptist: when his disciples said everyone was going to Jesus, he called it the fulfilment of his joy.
To be able to say “I must decrease” without bitterness is enormous freedom.
Reminder: hiddenness is not passivity, nor pretending to be terrible.

brief21.title: 5c. The Kingdom: Only Jesus
notes: They saw no one, except Jesus alone
Matthew 17:8
That they may glorify your Father in heaven
Matthew 5:16
Key points:
The Transfiguration: in Matthew 17:4 Peter wants to make three tents, putting Jesus on a level with Moses and Elijah.
When the cloud lifted, “they saw no one, except Jesus alone” — God himself removed the supporting actors.
Matthew 5:16: the light is to shine before people and be seen, but the end point is glory to the Father in heaven.
Psychology: Paul Piff, Dacher Keltner and colleagues, 2015, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology — awe brings a sense of the “small self” and actually increases altruism.
321 application: the 920 practice — before every “2,” live out the selfless “0,” bearing the ninefold fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23).

brief21.title: Practices 1 and 2
notes: Ask afterwards: for Jesus or for me?
Once a week, deliberate hiddenness
Give anonymously; credit the team
Your Father who sees in secret (Matthew 6:4)
Key points:
Exercise 1: at three set times a day, ask, “Did this give Jesus the glory, or give me satisfaction?”
Set three reminders on your phone, each titled “For whom?”
Exercise 2: once a week, one act of deliberate hiddenness — an anonymous gift, service you don’t post about, letting someone else present your good idea.
Matthew 6:3–4: don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does; your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
Evaluation: afterwards, does your heart feel light or resentful? Where we feel resentful is where we are still competing with God for the glory.

brief21.title: Practice 3 and the Eight Stages
notes: Ask each other with a spiritual companion
Did you let Jesus receive the glory this week?
Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation
Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication
Key points:
Exercise 3: three fixed weekly questions with a spiritual companion — where I stepped back, where I stole glory, where I will hide next week.
Proverbs 27:17, “Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.”
The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Stress: a mindset is not changed by a single flash of insight but by repetition; suggest twenty-one days in a row.
Multiplication: each bring along one more person, becoming the “3” of the 235 relationships, and finally establishing the “5,” a fivefold-ministry team.

brief21.title: Summing Up the 3-2-1 Vision
notes: Three Foundations: role model, standard, guide
Two Core Values: King, and all the glory
The Goal: establish God’s system
Everyone a channel; no one a reservoir
Key points:
The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.
The Two Core Values cannot be separated: kingship is about sovereignty, glory is about the goal.
The Goal: establish God’s system. In the human system glory flows to the top; in God’s system glory flows to Jesus.
1 Peter 5:5–6: exalting is God’s work; humbling ourselves is our work.
The priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, finally with things.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: What we are, can do, accomplish, bear
All his creation and provision
Don’t seize, share or hoard the glory
All the glory, wholly to Jesus
Key points:
The four “what we…”: what we are, can do, accomplish and bear — all of it is his.
1 Corinthians 15:10, “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.”
Psalm 115:1 repeats “not to us” twice: once the mind’s acknowledgement, once the heart’s surrender.
Call: only when the glory returns to him will revival come to the church; only when we are willing to be hidden will his beauty be seen.
Invite a resolution: Lord, not me but you be seen.

brief21.title: Response Prayer and Blessing
notes: Lord, not me but you be seen
Not for me but for you
All the glory, wholly to you
May the Lord bless you and keep you
Key points:
Lead the brothers and sisters in praying together; slow the pace and leave pauses.
Confession: giving God the glory with our lips while keeping a little for ourselves in our hearts.
Ask the Holy Spirit to shine light on hidden motives and give the courage to be gladly hidden and a heart big enough to cheer for others.
Close with the blessing of Numbers 6:24–26: “Yahweh bless you, and keep you.”

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to the second of the 3-2-1 vision’s Core Values: let Jesus receive all the glory. Let’s first read the key verse. Romans 11:36 says: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” In the last lesson we talked about “let Jesus be King” — a choice about sovereignty. Today we talk about “let Jesus receive the glory” — the direction and the goal of our lives. Sovereignty answers the question, “Who rules?” The goal answers the question, “Who am I living for?” And the answer to both is Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, let me start with a story. In eighteenth-century Germany there was a church organist named Bach. He had a habit: at the top of his manuscripts he wrote J. J., meaning “Jesus, help me”; and at the end he wrote S. D. G., meaning “To God alone be the glory.” At the beginning he asked Jesus for help; at the end he gave the glory to God. Let me ask you: if everything you did today had to be signed with initials, what would you sign? So often what we sign are three invisible words: “Look at me.” The battle over glory isn’t fought over big things; it’s fought over small things.

Let’s look at the background. The author of Romans is Paul, writing from Corinth around AD 56. The church in Rome was a mix of Jewish and Gentile believers, and the two groups kept comparing who mattered more. Paul spends chapters 9 to 11 laying out God’s plan of salvation, and when he has finished, what does he do? He doesn’t hand out a league table — he worships. The original is beautiful: “of him” is the source; “through him” is the channel; “to him” is the goal. All of it is him. Brothers and sisters, we are not at either end of that line; we are created things held within it.

The first key point: the focus of glory can have no one else in it. Isaiah 42:8 says: “I am Yahweh. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another.” God not sharing his glory is not pettiness; it is truthfulness. Brothers and sisters, have you ever looked at the moon at night? The moon is beautiful, but it doesn’t give off a single ray of its own light; all the moonlight we admire is the sun’s light. 2 Corinthians 3:18 says we see the Lord’s glory “as in a mirror.” We are reflectors, not light sources. The greatest failure of a mirror is when it begins to think the light is its own.

The second key point: serving is not about people seeing us, but about them seeing Jesus. Jesus said, “He who has seen me has seen the Father.” (John 14:9) Paul said, “So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:7) The Corinthian church was splitting into factions at the time — and what did Paul do? He took his own name down off the signboard. Brothers and sisters, our service is the window, not the view. A window doesn’t exist to be looked at, but to let the light in. If someone walks into a room and says, “What a beautiful window,” it usually means the window is blocking the view.

The third key point: stealing glory is a grave spiritual offence. Exodus 20:5 says: “For I, Yahweh your God, am a jealous God.” This jealousy is not pettiness; it is the exclusive devotion of covenant love. Why did Satan fall? Isaiah 14 records that he said “I will” five times, wanting to make himself like the Most High. His sin wasn’t murder or stealing money; it was wanting a weight that didn’t belong to him. Acts 12:23 says: “Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory.” Brothers and sisters, 321 puts it very precisely: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

The fourth key point: earthly glory is temporary; only heavenly glory is eternal. When Jesus spoke about giving, praying and fasting, three times he said the same thing: “Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.” (Matthew 6:2) In the original this was a commercial term meaning “paid in full,” just like stamping “PAID” on a receipt. Brothers and sisters, you wanted people’s applause? Fine — you’ve received it. The account is settled, and heaven owes you nothing more. Earthly glory is like fireworks: very bright, very beautiful, gone in three seconds. Heavenly glory is like the stars: it doesn’t dazzle, but it shines for ever and ever. Do you want to be a three-second firework, or a star for ever?

The fifth key point: selflessness, hiddenness and the kingdom are all so that the glory goes to Jesus. Selflessness is letting the self step down: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Hiddenness is being willing not to be seen; John the Baptist said, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” The kingdom means not building an empire for ourselves; the Lord’s Prayer says, “Let your Kingdom come.” At the Transfiguration, Peter wanted to make three tents, putting Jesus on a level with Moses and Elijah; when the cloud lifted, “they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” God himself removed every supporting actor, because the focus of glory can have no one else in it.

Let’s set today’s message back into the 3-2-1 vision. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he said, “I don’t seek my own glory”; the Bible is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide, shining light on our hidden motives. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, in the human system, glory flows to the one person at the top; in God’s system, glory passes through every person and flows to Jesus. Everyone is a channel; no one is a reservoir.

Next, three exercises. First, after everything you do, ask: was this to glorify Jesus, or to glorify me? Second, once a week, choose one act of deliberate hiddenness — an anonymous gift, an act of service you don’t post about, letting someone else present your good idea. Third, ask each other with your spiritual companion: did you let Jesus receive the glory this week? 321 says there are eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Brothers and sisters, a mindset isn’t changed by a single flash of insight, but by repetition. Please start today and practise for twenty-one days in a row.

Brothers and sisters, what we are is his creation; what we can do is his gift; what we accomplish is his using us; the fruit we bear is his provision. Paul said, “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10) That being so, let us not seize the glory, not share the glory, not hoard the glory, but give all the glory, wholly, to Jesus. Only when the glory returns to him will revival come to the church; only when we are willing to be hidden will the beauty of Jesus be seen. Will you make that resolution today?

Let’s pray together. Lord Jesus, we acknowledge that all things are of you, through you and to you. Forgive us: with our lips we give you the glory, yet in our hearts we so often secretly keep a little for ourselves. Holy Spirit, shine your light on our hidden motives; give us the courage to be gladly hidden, and a heart big enough to cheer for others. Lord, not me but you be seen; not for me but for you; all the glory, wholly to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray, Amen. “Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you.” Brothers and sisters, peace be with you today.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. May the peace of the Lord be with you. In this morning’s reading we will enter together into the second of the 3-2-1 vision’s Core Values: let Jesus receive all the glory. Let’s first read the key verse. Romans 11:36 says: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” In the last lesson we talked about the first Core Value, let Jesus be King — a choice about sovereignty. Today we talk about direction and goal. Sovereignty answers the question, “Who rules?” The goal answers the question, “Who am I living for?” Brothers and sisters, both questions have only one answer — Jesus.

First I want to ask you to picture a scene in your mind. Germany, the eighteenth century. A church organist sits at his desk, finishing off a stack of freshly written music. His name is Bach. Music history has kept a moving detail about him: at the top of his manuscripts Bach habitually wrote J. J., short for the Latin “Jesus, help me”; and at the end of a manuscript he would write S. D. G., meaning “To God alone be the glory.” At the beginning, he asked Jesus for help; at the end, he gave the glory to God. The hundreds of pages of notes in between are among the greatest works in the history of human music. And yet the man who wrote them knew perfectly well: this is not my monument; this is a gift offered to God.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask you: if everything you did today — the report you write, the meal you cook, the Bible study you lead, every message you type in the group chat — had to be signed at the end with a set of initials, what would you sign? Some would sign “To God alone be the glory”; some would sign their own name. And more often than not, what we sign is a set of invisible letters: “Please notice me,” “Please remember it was me who did this.” Psychology holds up a very honest mirror here. In a 1981 study, the Swedish psychologist Ola Svenson found that among the American drivers he tested, around 93 per cent believed their driving skill was better than the median. Statistically, that is impossible. Overrating ourselves is not the flaw of a few; it is the default setting of the whole human race.

Let’s first look at the background. The author of Romans is the apostle Paul, writing around AD 56–57 in Corinth in Greece. The church in Rome was not founded by Paul; it was a mixture of Jewish and Gentile believers, and there was real tension between the two groups. Acts 18:2 mentions that the emperor Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome; later, as Jewish believers gradually returned, the question arose: “Who matters more?” Paul spends chapters 9 to 11 laying out God’s plan of salvation from beginning to end. And when he has finished, what does he do? He doesn’t hand out a league table — he worships. The original is beautiful: “of him” is the source; “through him” is the channel; “to him” is the goal. And the word “glory” — in Hebrew, kabod — has the root meaning “weight.” To give someone glory is to acknowledge who truly carries weight.

We come to the first key point: the focus of glory can have no one else in it. Isaiah 42:8 says: “I am Yahweh. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to engraved images.” Brothers and sisters, God doesn’t share his glory, not because he is petty, but because he is truthful. If a god were to share his glory with false gods, he would be conceding that false gods also deserve worship. Colossians 1:16 says: “All things have been created through him and for him.” Notice the words “and for him.” You were not created to fulfil your dreams, but to fulfil his purposes.

Let me use an illustration. Brothers and sisters, have you ever looked up at the moon at night? The moon is beautiful and bright; countless poems down the ages and across the world have praised it. But here is a fact about the moon: it does not give off a single ray of its own light. According to NASA, the moon’s surface has an albedo of only about 12 per cent; all the moonlight we admire is the sun’s light. The moon has never felt inferior about this, and it has never claimed the credit either; it simply stands quietly in the right place. 2 Corinthians 3:18 says we see the Lord’s glory “as in a mirror.” We are reflectors, not light sources. The greatest failure of a mirror is to think the light is its own.

The second key point: serving is not about people seeing us, but about them seeing Jesus. Philip asked Jesus to show them the Father, and Jesus replied, “He who has seen me has seen the Father.” (John 14:9) Glory was rightly Jesus’ own, but look at how he prays. John 17:4 says: “I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do.” His summary of his own life was not “Look how much ministry I’ve accomplished,” but “I glorified you.” Paul also said: “So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:7) The Corinthian church was splitting into factions at the time — how did Paul deal with it? He took his own name down off the signboard.

1 Corinthians 4:7 lands an even heavier blow: “And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast?” Brothers and sisters, your gifts were received; your opportunities were received; your health, your intelligence, your eloquence, your time — all received. Nothing received can ever be grounds for boasting. I love this illustration: a good servant is like a window. A window does not exist to be looked at, but to let the light in. If someone walks into a room and the first thing they say is, “What a beautiful window,” it usually means the window is blocking the view. Even management research can see it. In Good to Great, Jim Collins found that the best leaders share a trait he called “the window and the mirror”: when things succeed, they look out of the window and give the credit to others; when things fail, they look in the mirror and take responsibility themselves. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

The third key point: stealing glory is a grave spiritual offence. Exodus 20:5 says: “For I, Yahweh your God, am a jealous God.” In the original, “jealous” is the language of covenant love: a husband’s exclusive love for his wife will, by its very nature, not tolerate a third party. God is jealous not because he is petty, but because his love is exclusive. Why did Satan fall? Isaiah 14:13–14 records: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!” Count them — in these verses there are five “I will”s. His sin was wanting a weight that didn’t belong to him. 321 puts it with great precision: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take the place of God.

The Bible gives us two fearful examples. The first is Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Daniel 4:30 records him saying: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” And while the words were still in the king’s mouth, a voice came down from heaven; he was driven away from people and ate grass like an ox. The second is King Herod. Acts 12:23 says: “Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.” This Herod Agrippa I died in AD 44. Brothers and sisters, if we, by grace, are used by God, but then turn to exalting ourselves, could we fall into the same danger?

When people do not give glory to God, they become foolish and corrupt. Romans 1:21 says: “Because knowing God, they didn’t glorify him as God, and didn’t give thanks, but became vain in their reasoning, and their senseless heart was darkened.” Look at the cause and effect here: failing to glorify God is the cause; a darkened mind is the effect. The first punishment for stealing glory is not a bolt from the blue, but a mind that begins to grow muddled. Psychology bears this out too. In their 2004 paper “The Costly Pursuit of Self-Esteem,” Crocker and Park showed that when people build their self-worth on outside approval, over the long run they pay a price — their motivation declines, their relationships suffer, their health is affected. Because they have to keep winning; the moment the applause stops, they collapse. This is exactly what makes the self-centred life so exhausting: you have to carry your own glory yourself — and you can’t carry it.

The fourth key point: earthly glory is temporary; only heavenly glory is eternal. Matthew 6:2 on giving, 6:5 on prayer and 6:16 on fasting all end with the same conclusion: “Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.” In the original, “have received” was a commercial term of the day meaning “paid in full,” just like the “PAID” stamped on a receipt. Jesus’ meaning is: you wanted people’s applause? Fine — you’ve already received it. The account is settled, and heaven owes you nothing more. John 12:43 says: “for they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise.”

Brothers and sisters, we’ve all seen fireworks. A rocket shoots up and bursts across the night sky, dazzling, and the whole crowd gasps. And then? Three seconds later there is nothing left but a wisp of smoke and paper scattered on the ground. Earthly glory is like fireworks: extremely bright, extremely beautiful, extremely short. And what is heavenly glory like? Like starlight. Starlight doesn’t dazzle, yet it has already been shining for millions of years, and it will keep on shining. Daniel 12:3 says: “Those who turn many to righteousness will shine as the stars forever and ever.” In the eighteenth century some of the Moravian Brethren sold themselves into slavery simply to be able to live among slaves and preach the gospel. The words generally said to have spurred them on were: “May the Lamb that was slain receive the reward of his suffering.” No one remembers their names, yet the fire they lit has burned for three hundred years. Do you want to be a three-second firework, or a star for ever and ever?

The fifth key point has three aspects: selflessness, hiddenness and the kingdom. First, selflessness. Galatians 2:20 says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” 321 stresses again and again: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living it out. A cup full of itself has no room for anything else; a life emptied of itself gives God room to fill it. Philippians 2 says that Christ emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death. He went down, and God raised him up — and the end point is “to the glory of God the Father.”

Second, hiddenness. Colossians 3:3 says: “For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” John the Baptist is the model of hiddenness. When his disciples told him that everyone was going to Jesus, he did not defend his territory; he said: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30) To be able to say “I must decrease” without bitterness in your heart is enormous freedom. But hiddenness is not passivity, and it is not pretending to be terrible. True hiddenness is this: I give it everything, I do it beautifully, and then I let that beauty point to Jesus.

Third, the kingdom. At the Transfiguration, Peter said something very human: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. Let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” Then a cloud overshadowed them, and a voice said: “This is my beloved Son. Listen to him.” When the cloud lifted, Matthew 17:8 says: “they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” God himself removed every supporting actor. So are we never to be seen at all? No. Jesus said: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16) The light is to be seen, but the glory is to go to the Father. A 2015 study by Piff, Keltner and colleagues found that when people experience awe, they feel a sense of the “small self” — and become more generous and more willing to give. The bigger Jesus becomes, the smaller we become; and the smaller we become, the freer we are.

Now for three practical exercises. Exercise one: after everything you do, ask — was this to glorify Jesus, or to glorify me? I suggest you set three reminders on your phone — midday, early evening and before bed — each titled “For whom?” Exercise two: once a week, choose one act of deliberate hiddenness. When you perform well, don’t talk about it; simply offer thanks in prayer. Give the glory to the team. Quietly help someone else succeed without asking to be noticed. Jesus said: “Your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.” (Matthew 6:4) Afterwards, check honestly: does your heart feel light or resentful? The places where we feel resentful are the places where we are still competing with God for the glory.

Exercise three: ask each other with your spiritual companion — did you let Jesus receive the glory this week? Each week ask the same three questions: Where this week did I choose to step back? Where did I carelessly steal the Lord’s glory and need to repent? In what situation next week am I willing to choose to hide myself? Proverbs 27:17 says: “Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.” 321 says there are eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. A mindset isn’t changed by a single flash of insight, but by repetition. Please start today and practise for twenty-one days in a row.

Let’s set what we have learned today back into the whole of the 3-2-1 vision. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he said, “I don’t seek my own glory”; the Bible is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide, shining light on our hidden motives. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The two cannot be separated — you cannot let Jesus reign as King while collecting the glory for yourself. The Goal: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, in the human system, glory flows upwards to the one person at the top; in God’s system, glory passes through every person and flows upwards to Jesus. Everyone is a channel; no one is a reservoir. 1 Peter 5:6 says: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” Exalting is God’s work; humbling ourselves is our work.

Brothers and sisters, we’ve come to the end. What we are is his creation; what we can do is his gift; what we accomplish is his using us; the fruit we bear is his provision. Paul put it most honestly: “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10) That being so, let us not seize the glory, not share the glory, not hoard the glory, but give all the glory, wholly, to Jesus. Psalm 115:1 says: “Not to us, Yahweh, not to us, but to your name give glory, for your loving kindness, and for your truth’s sake.” “Not to us” is repeated twice: the first time is the mind’s acknowledgement; the second is the heart’s surrender. Only when the glory returns to him will revival come to the church.

Will you resolve today and say: “Lord, not me but you be seen; not for me but for you; all the glory, wholly to you”? Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we worship you. We acknowledge that all things are of you, through you and to you. Lord, forgive us. So often we give you the glory with our lips while secretly keeping a little for ourselves in our hearts; we long to be seen when we serve, and we grow bitter when we are overlooked. Wash us with your precious blood. Holy Spirit, shine your light on our hidden motives; give us the courage to be gladly hidden, and a heart big enough to cheer for others. Make our lives a clean window, so that when people look through us, what they see is not us, but you. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. “Yahweh bless you, and keep you.” Brothers and sisters, peace be with you today.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: Two Cities, Two Ways of Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This early morning, I’d like to ask you first to be still for one minute and recall every little decision you made yesterday.

Yesterday at the office, when someone claimed the credit for themselves, what was your first reaction inside? Last night, when someone in your family said something cutting, did you choose to answer back, or did you choose to stay quiet?

Each of these things is small — so small that we would never write them down in our prayer journal. But brothers and sisters, here is a spiritual secret: you don’t decide which kingdom you belong to in one great battle. You hand yourself over to one kingdom or the other, bit by bit, through a thousand small choices.

In AD 410 the city of Rome was captured, and the whole Mediterranean world was thrown into terror. In that shaken era Augustine wrote The City of God, and in Book 14, chapter 28, he wrote words that would shape Europe for fifteen hundred years: two loves have made two cities; love of self, even to the contempt of God, made the earthly city; love of God, even to the contempt of self, made the heavenly city.

Two loves, two cities. This is the single thread that runs through the Bible from Genesis to Revelation: throughout human history two systems have always run side by side — one is the Babylonian system, the other is God’s system.

We have already walked through six lessons together: from the end-times call to “come out of Babylon,” to how to overcome the Babylonian system, and then laying the Three Foundations one stone at a time — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide — and then gripping the Two Core Values firmly: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

Today we come to the final link of the 321 vision, the destination to which all the foundations and core values are ultimately pointing — the Goal: establish God’s system.

Brothers and sisters, the Three Foundations are not three pieces of knowledge, and the Two Core Values are not two slogans; they are building materials — the steel and the concrete — and they are meant to be built into something. If you have learned the Three Foundations and memorised the Two Core Values but have no Goal, all you have in your hands is a pile of materials scattered on the ground, and no house.

God has never been only about tearing down; God is about building up. He calls us out of Babylon, not to leave us standing in the wilderness in the wind, but to establish a system that belongs to him — in us, in our families and in our fellowship.

Today we are going to see seven things together: why we must establish God’s system; that even in Babylon we can live out the pattern of God’s kingdom; that the key lies in every single choice; that the pattern of action is know — do — receive; that falling down doesn’t matter, because when you get up you can move forward; and the point that sets us most free of all — living out 321 is not by effort but by grace; and finally, how habits become a system, and the system becomes life. Let’s build our house on the rock together.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: What Is Babylon? And What Is God’s System?
sections.html:
To understand the call to “come out of Babylon,” we first have to get to know Babylon.

1. Babylon in history

Historically, Babylon lay on the banks of the Euphrates, about eighty kilometres south of present-day Baghdad in Iraq. Nebuchadnezzar II, who reigned from 605 to 562 BC, built it into the most magnificent city of the ancient world: the empire’s wealth, military power, religion and culture were all concentrated in this one city.

For the people of the Bible, Babylon was an agonising memory. In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar first took Jerusalem and carried off a group of young nobles, among them Daniel and his three friends; in 586 BC Jerusalem fell, the temple was burned, and the kingdom of Judah came to an end.

But brothers and sisters, the Bible’s concern with Babylon has never been merely political history.

2. Babylon in the spiritual sense

The name Babylon first appears as Babel in Genesis 11. “They said, ‘Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth.’” (Genesis 11:4)

Look at the three key phrases in this verse: “let’s build ourselves,” “let’s make a name for ourselves,” “lest we be scattered” — people want to build by themselves, people want to make their own name great, people seek security in themselves. This is the DNA of the Babylonian system; in the language of 321, it is the self-centred life: making self the centre, self the glory and self the safeguard. The lesson puts it very precisely: “Babylon means every system that is worldly, centred on man and set against God.”

Today’s Babylon has no gates of glazed brick, but it takes more refined forms: the set of values that tells you to “fight your way to the top for yourself,” the scoring system that measures a person’s worth by performance, looks and the number of likes, the rhythm of life that, without your noticing, puts God in the very last slot of your diary.

3. Three calls to “come out”

Three times the Bible calls God’s people to “come out,” each time going deeper than the last.

The first is a geographical coming out. Isaiah 48:20: “Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans! With a voice of singing announce this, tell it even to the end of the earth: say, ‘Yahweh has redeemed his servant Jacob!’” In 538 BC Cyrus king of Persia issued his decree, fulfilling this call.

The second is a moral and spiritual coming out. 2 Corinthians 6:17: “Therefore ‘Come out from among them, and be separate,’ says the Lord. ‘Touch no unclean thing. I will receive you.’” People may already be in grace, and yet their hearts may still be lingering in Babylon.

The third is the final, end-times coming out. Revelation 18:4: “Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues.” The apostle John wrote Revelation on the island of Patmos in the 90s AD. At that time it was the Roman Empire that was oppressing the church, yet the Holy Spirit did not use the name “Rome”; he used “Babylon” — because Babylon is not a place name in the past tense; it is a system that exists in every generation.

Pay special attention to two words in Revelation 18:4: “my people.” Those God calls out are his own people. A person can already be saved and still be living inside the Babylonian system; can already be a child of God and still think in the patterns of Babel. That is why we need this lesson.

4. God’s system: God has always been building

So what is it that God wants us to establish?

Ephesians 2:20–22: “being built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone; in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit.”

“Built together” in the original is συνοικοδομεῖσθε, formed from “together” plus “to build a house,” and it is in the passive voice — it is not that we build ourselves; we are “being” built together. This grammatical detail is the key to this lesson: God’s system is not something people build for God; it is what God builds in us by the Holy Spirit. Our part is to obey — every day to place this living stone that is ourselves into his hands. 1 Peter 2:5 also says: “You also, as living stones, are built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.”

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Babylon says, “Let’s build ourselves a city”; God says, “You also are built together.” Babylon’s verb is the active “I build”; the kingdom’s verb is the passive “being built.” One is the self-centred life; the other is selflessness. One wants to make our own name great; the other wants Jesus to receive all the glory.

And Psalm 127:1 wrote the conclusion out plainly long ago: “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.”

sections.heading: 3. Key Point 1: The Only Way Out of Babylon Is to Establish God’s System
sections.html:
The lesson opens by saying that God’s call to his people — “come out of Babylon” — is not a geographical relocation but a change of spiritual system.

Brothers and sisters, that sentence is worth a lifetime of meditation. Because our most common mistake is to understand “coming out” as “leaving a certain place.”

The Israelites are the best example. It took God one night, through Moses, to bring them out of Egypt; but it took forty years to bring Egypt out of them. Numbers 11:5 records their complaint: “We remember the fish, which we ate in Egypt for nothing; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlic.” The people came out; the system did not.

In the same way, we may have been baptised for years, we may already be serving in the fellowship, and yet still be living our days the Babylonian way: measuring our worth by comparison, protecting our position by manoeuvring, numbing the emptiness inside with busyness.

Why isn’t “leaving” enough? Why must we “establish”?

The Lord Jesus told a sobering parable. Matthew 12:43–44: “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he passes through waterless places, seeking rest, and doesn’t find it. Then he says, ‘I will return into my house from which I came out,’ and when he has come back, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order.”

Notice the word “empty.” The house had been swept clean, but it was empty; and an empty house cannot be held. As a result, verse 45 says, the last state of that man became worse than the first.

So “coming out” alone is not enough. You can’t just clear out; you must move in. You can’t just tear down; you must build.

The lesson says it clearly: “To truly escape Babylon, the only way out is to establish God’s system, with Christ at its centre.”

When do we slide back into Babylon?

The lesson gives an extremely precise diagnosis: “When people leave the Three Foundations and the Two Core Values, they naturally fall into the Worldly system and use their own methods to build a human kingdom.”

Notice the word “naturally.” Falling into Babylon takes no effort, just as a house gathers dust without any effort and a garden grows weeds without any effort. Spiritual desolation is not a sudden event; it is a stretch of time when no one is keeping watch.

Conversely, the lesson also gives the remedy: “As long as we return every day to the Three Foundations — letting Jesus be our role model, letting the Bible be our standard, letting the Holy Spirit be our guide — together with the Two Core Values — letting Jesus be King and letting Jesus receive the glory — we are establishing God’s system.”

Listen carefully to the tense of that verb: “we are establishing.” Not “we will establish one day,” but “we are establishing right now.” The moment you opened your Bible this morning, you were establishing it; the moment at noon today when you swallow a retort you wanted to fire back, you are establishing it.

An everyday illustration: two builders

At the end of the Sermon on the Mount the Lord Jesus said (Matthew 7:24–25): “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.”

Both men built houses. On a sunny day they may have looked exactly the same; the one on the sand may even have gone up faster and looked better. The difference lay below ground, where no one could see.

Brothers and sisters, your spiritual system is that “below ground”: it’s your fifteen minutes alone with God early in the morning, your honesty when no one is watching, your obedience in the small things. On a sunny day you can’t see the difference; when the storm comes, the difference is everything.

Applying 321: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective

The 321 vision says we must go through a fourfold shift of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. The Babylonian system is man’s, earthly, temporary and worldly; God’s system is God’s, heavenly, eternal and godly. 2 Corinthians 4:18 says: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.”

So the first step in establishing God’s system is not changing behaviour but changing the mindset. Romans 12:2 says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” The root of the original word for “conformed” carries the sense of “a mould, a pattern,” while “transformed” is μεταμορφοῦσθε — the “metamorphosis” by which a caterpillar becomes a butterfly. God does not want us to touch up the mould of Babylon; he wants us to exchange our whole life from the inside out — and that is exactly 321’s fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry.

sections.heading: 4. Key Point 2: Even in Babylon, We Can Live Out the Pattern of God’s Kingdom
sections.html:
At this point some of you may be thinking: “Pastor, I understand the teaching, but my office is Babylon, my extended family is Babylon — I simply can’t get out.”

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the second part of the lesson answers: “Although Daniel and his three friends lived in Babylon, they chose not to be defiled and not to compromise, and they held fast to their reverence for God and their loyalty to him.”

Daniel: holding to the first choice in the king’s palace

In 605 BC, when Daniel was taken captive, he was probably only in his teens. He was brought into Nebuchadnezzar’s palace. His name was changed — Daniel (meaning “God is my judge”) became Belteshazzar. He was taught the language and learning of the Chaldeans for three years. He was assigned the king’s food and the king’s wine. New surroundings, new name, new education, new diet: a complete programme of system re-engineering.

Daniel could not choose his surroundings, could not refuse the new name, could not skip the classes. But the Bible records the one thing he could choose — Daniel 1:8: “But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.”

The Hebrew behind “purposed” literally means “to set it upon the heart” (sim al-lev). Brothers and sisters, God’s system is established starting from the heart, not from the environment. Daniel could not change Babylon, but inside Babylon he could draw a line and say: this step I will not take.

And the result? A man who held on to God’s system inside Babylon went on to stand firm through three successive regimes.

The three friends: holding to “but if not” before the furnace

In Daniel 3, Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden image and ordered the whole nation to fall down and worship it. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego stayed standing and would not kneel. The king was furious and ordered them to be thrown into the burning fiery furnace.

Their reply is one of the most courageous declarations of faith in the Old Testament. Daniel 3:17–18: “If it happens, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace; and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image which you have set up.”

“But if not” — those three words are the touchstone of God’s system. Many people believe in God because of what God will do for them; that kind of faith is still Babylonian, because the centre is still “me.” “But if not” faith says: even if God doesn’t do what I want, I will still serve him. That is selflessness; that is letting Jesus be King.

In the end God did not rescue them out of the fire; he was with them in the fire. In Daniel 3:25 the king said in astonishment: “Look, I see four men loose, walking in the middle of the fire, and they are unharmed. The appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods.”

The lesson says: “Though they were in a foreign land, they lived out the light of God’s system, so that everyone saw the glory of God.” Exactly so — Nebuchadnezzar, a pagan king, finally said in Daniel 4:37: “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven.”

Daniel’s secret: habit

Daniel 6:10 records a hugely important detail: “When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.”

Notice the last words: “as he did before.”

Brothers and sisters, what Daniel did in the crisis of the lions’ den was not a burst of last-minute heroics but a habit kept unchanged for decades. When the crisis came, he didn’t need to decide whether to pray, because he had decided long before; he simply had to do what he always did. That is the power of a system: when pressure comes, you don’t make your choice on the strength of willpower in the moment; you respond naturally out of a structure built up over a long time.

In his Principles of Psychology, published in 1890, the psychologist William James wrote that habit is the enormous flywheel of society. It takes a great deal of force to get a flywheel turning, but once it is turning, it is hard to stop. God’s system is that flywheel in our lives.

Applying 321: life first, then relationships, then ministry

Daniel didn’t launch a religious reformation the moment he entered the palace. First he guarded his own relationship with God (life); then he won the trust of the chief of the eunuchs (relationships); only last was he promoted to govern the affairs of the kingdom (ministry).

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry; and the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and finally with things. We often reverse the order: rushing to do things without life, rushing to change others without first being changed by God — and so the bigger the ministry, the drier the life. Daniel’s example is this: first settle your heart, and leave the rest to God.

sections.heading: 5. Key Point 3: The Key to Establishing God’s System Lies in Every Single Choice
sections.html:
The lesson says something very striking: “A system is not a one-off decision but the accumulation of countless choices.”

Then the lesson lists three pairs of questions, and I’d like you to take them to heart:

Will I choose to indulge myself, or choose to let Jesus be King?

Will I choose to act on my feelings, or obey the principles of the Bible?

Will I choose to put myself on display, or let Jesus receive the glory?

And then the lesson draws a conclusion that is one of the golden sayings of this lesson: “Choose once, and it has an effect; choose countless times, and it forms a system; let the system run long enough, and it becomes life.”

The witness of the Bible: choosing is the Bible’s repeated call

The Bible never treats people as machines; it is always calling people to choose.

Moses said on the plains of Moab (Deuteronomy 30:19): “I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse. Therefore choose life, that you may live, you and your descendants.” Joshua said at Shechem (Joshua 24:15): “but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.” Elijah asked on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:21): “How long will you waver between the two sides? If Yahweh is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him.”

Brothers and sisters, God never forces you into his system. He respects your choice, because love must be free.

Choices in small things are the real choices

The Lord Jesus said in Luke 16:10: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.”

We often imagine that the decisive spiritual moments are the big scenes: whether to change jobs, whether to give ourselves to full-time ministry, whether to forgive the person who hurt us deeply. But the truth is, by the time the big scene arrives, your response has long since been decided by your choices in a thousand small scenes.

In a study published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, the University College London psychologist Phillippa Lally and her colleagues followed ninety-six participants as they formed new habits and found that it took an average of sixty-six days for a behaviour to become automatic, with individual differences ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days; and missing an occasional day along the way did not significantly damage the formation of the habit.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? A spiritual system takes time; one slip will not destroy your system — only giving up will.

An everyday illustration: how a riverbed is formed

Have you ever seen muddy ground after a heavy rain? Where the water has flowed, it leaves a shallow trace, and the next time water comes it flows that way more easily; the more it flows, the deeper the channel, until finally a riverbed is formed. Neuroscience tells us the brain works the same way: when a group of neurons fire together repeatedly, the axons connecting them are wrapped layer upon layer in myelin, and signals travel dramatically faster.

Brothers and sisters, every time you choose to let Jesus be King, you are digging one channel deeper in your life; every time you choose to indulge yourself, you are digging another one deeper. The question is not whether you are digging, but which channel you’re digging.

Applying 321: Jesus is the focal point

321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. Why does every choice matter so much? Because every choice is an adjustment of our focus. When Peter was walking on the water, the Bible says (Matthew 14:30): “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink.” He didn’t begin to sink because the waves got bigger; he began to sink because he looked at the waves and not at the Lord. May every choice we make be a movement of turning our eyes back to Jesus.

sections.heading: 6. Key Point 4: The 321 Pattern of Action — Know, Do, Receive
sections.html:
The lesson says: “To establish God’s system, it isn’t enough just to know; you have to do it in order to receive it.”

Then the lesson lays out these three levels very clearly: knowing the principles of 321 is only the beginning; truly living out the 321 life is the key; and as you keep making these choices again and again, the 321 system becomes internalised as part of your life — and you have received God’s system.

Knowing: information is not life

James 1:22 says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.”

“Deluding your own selves” in the original carries the sense of “deceiving by false reasoning.” What is the false reasoning? Treating “I understand it” as if it meant “I’ve done it.”

Believers in our generation have heard more sermons than any generation in church history, but hearing much is not the same as growing well. Knowledge that doesn’t turn into obedience turns into pride. 1 Corinthians 8:1 says: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”

Doing: the Lord Jesus’ own standard

In Matthew 7:24 the Lord Jesus spoke of “everyone … who hears these words of mine, and does them.” He didn’t say “and nods,” nor “and takes notes.” In John 13:17, after washing his disciples’ feet, the Lord Jesus said: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” Notice the structure of the verse: know — do — be blessed. The blessing doesn’t lie between knowing and doing; the blessing comes after doing. Too many Christians stop on the empty ground in the middle and then ask in bewilderment: “Why don’t I experience God?”

Receiving: internalised into life

Hebrews 5:14: “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” The root of the original word for “exercised” is the word from which we get “gymnasium,” and it is in the perfect tense, describing an ongoing state produced by long training. Spiritual discernment doesn’t drop out of the sky; it is trained. 1 Timothy 4:7–8: “Exercise yourself toward godliness. For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things, having the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come.”

When you’re wrong, change

The lesson closes this section with a sentence full of a shepherd’s heart: “Don’t be afraid of mistakes; what is most to be feared is refusing to repent. Wherever in life you go off course, as long as you change when you’re wrong, you are still on God’s road.”

Brothers and sisters, memorise these three words: wrong? then change.

1 John 1:9: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” “Confess” in the original is ὁμολογῶμεν, meaning “to say the same thing” — to say the same thing as God. Repentance is not self-reproach, not stewing in regret at yourself; it is coming over to God’s side and admitting that he sees rightly.

“Repentance” in the New Testament is μετάνοια, which literally means “a change of mind.” This is exactly what 321 calls the first of the fivefold changes: a change of mindset.

Applying 321: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves

321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you fret, rely on the heart and you’re glad. If “know — do — receive” stays only in the head, it becomes a self-improvement programme — the most exhausting religion there is. Proverbs 4:23 says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” What we need is not to try harder, but to draw nearer.

sections.heading: 7. Key Point 5: Falling Down Doesn’t Matter — Get Up and You Can Move Forward
sections.html:
The lesson says: “In spiritual training we will certainly have times when we drift off course and fall, but this is nothing to be afraid of; the key is whether we are willing to choose again to return to 321.”

Then the lesson uses a very good comparison: “It is like learning to walk: losing your balance and falling is exactly the process of learning to be steady and move forward.”

A surprising statistic

In a study published in 2012 in the journal Psychological Science, the New York University psychologist Karen Adolph and her colleagues video-recorded more than a hundred infants who had just learned to walk, and found that a toddler takes on average about 2,368 steps an hour — and falls about seventeen times.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask you: has any baby ever fallen seventeen times and decided, “That’s it, I’m never walking again”? Never. For a baby, falling is not evidence of failure; falling is part of learning. And that study found that the children who walked more and fell more were actually the ones who improved fastest. Accumulated experience matters more than being careful.

How the Bible sees falling

Proverbs 24:16: “for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.”

The Bible doesn’t say the righteous never fall; it says that when the righteous fall, they “rise up again.” The difference between the righteous and the wicked is not whether they fall, but whether they get up.

Psalm 37:23–24: “A man’s steps are established by Yahweh. He delights in his way. Though he stumble, he shall not fall, for Yahweh holds him up with his hand.” The beauty of these verses is that they don’t deny we will stumble; they simply tell us there is a hand that is always holding us up. Micah 7:8 is even the declaration of a captive people among the ruins: “When I fall, I will arise. When I sit in darkness, Yahweh will be a light to me.”

Peter’s story

One of the disciples who fell hardest in the Bible was Peter: in the high priest’s courtyard he denied the Lord three times, and he went out and wept bitterly. If the story had stopped there, Peter would have been a failure. But after his resurrection the Lord Jesus lit a charcoal fire on the shore of the Sea of Tiberias — a charcoal fire just like the one in the courtyard on the night Peter fell — and three times asked him, “Do you love me more than these?” (John 21:15) Three falls, three restorations. The Lord was not humiliating Peter; he was restoring him. Not long afterwards, the man who had fallen stood up at Pentecost and preached, and three thousand people believed.

The lesson puts it superbly: “True failure is not falling down, but refusing to get up again.”

Applying 321: “Evaluation, Correction, Repetition” in the eight stages of changing our mindset

321’s eight stages of changing our mindset are: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Notice that “Evaluation” and “Correction” are written right into the process — in God’s design, falling and correcting are not accidents but a stop that has been planned for.

A system that does not allow failure is the Babylonian system, because it depends on human performance; a system that allows failure but does not allow giving up is God’s system, because it depends on God’s grace. Lamentations 3:22–23: “It is because of Yahweh’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his compassion doesn’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.” This is why we hold our morning devotion every morning — because his mercies are new every morning.

sections.heading: 8. Key Point 6: Living Out 321 Is Not by Effort, but by Grace
sections.html:
In this section the lesson says something almost counter-intuitive: “Many people say, ‘It sounds simple, but it’s hard to do.’ But in the practice of 321 it’s the other way round — it sounds simple, and it’s even simpler to do.”

Why? The lesson says: “Because it doesn’t depend on human willpower, but on God’s grace.”

Grace is not slackness; grace is power

First let me clear up a common misunderstanding: relying on grace does not mean doing nothing; relying on grace is about where the power to do it comes from.

Philippians 2:12–13 puts both sides in one sentence: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” Look at that word “for.” “Works” in the original is ἐνεργῶν, the source of the English word “energy,” meaning “to set energy in motion, to make effective.” God is not standing on the shore shouting encouragement; God is the engine running inside us.

1 Corinthians 15:10: “But by the grace of God I am what I am. … I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” Paul was the hardest-working man in the New Testament, and also the one who insisted most firmly, “not I, but the grace of God.” Hard work and grace are not in conflict; we simply need to be clear about the source.

The warning of Galatians

In Galatians 3:3 Paul rebukes the Galatians: “Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” What a precisely aimed jab: we were all saved by grace, yet we often try to become holy by our own strength, building God’s temple by Babylon’s methods. This is exactly the lesson’s warning: “If we are proud and self-righteous and try to establish a spiritual system by our own strength, we will in the end surely fail.”

An iron law of the spiritual life

The lesson says: “The humble receive grace; the proud are resisted. This is an iron law of the spiritual life.”

This comes from James 4:6, which reads: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” 1 Peter 5:5 says the same.

“Resists” in the original is ἀντιτάσσεται, a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against, to set the ranks in opposition.” Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: God does not merely dislike pride; God draws up his battle lines against pride.

Why? 321 puts it well: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. What’s more, pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility inspires humility and both sides win.

Why is it “even simpler to do” for the humble?

Because the humble don’t have to carry the burden of “I have to prove myself.”

The Lord Jesus said in Matthew 11:28–30: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

In the ancient world a yoke was often a double yoke: on one side a strong, mature ox, on the other a young ox still learning, and the one really pulling the plough was the strong one. When the Lord says, “Take my yoke,” he means: come, get in the harness beside me, and I’ll do the pulling.

The English writer C. S. Lewis, in Mere Christianity, describes the truly humble person: when you meet him, all you will think is that he seemed to take a real interest in what you said to him; he will not be thinking about humility, because he will not be thinking about himself at all.

Brothers and sisters, this is what 321 calls “selflessness”: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.”

Applying 321: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan

The core message of 321 says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Satan’s fall was pride. Isaiah 14:13–14: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!’” Did you notice that string of “I will”s? That is the manifesto of the self-centred life.

The Lord Jesus is the opposite. Philippians 2:6–8: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” “Emptied himself” in the original is ἐκένωσεν, “he poured himself out” — the most perfect definition of selflessness.

Brothers and sisters, we cannot become humble by trying harder, because “striving to be humble” can itself very easily become another form of pride. All we can do is come to Jesus and let his life be lived out in us.

sections.heading: 9. Integrating the 321 Vision: Everything Is for This One Goal
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, having come this far, let’s spread out the whole map of 321 and look at it once more.

The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal is: establish God’s system.

Notice the logic of this structure: the Three Foundations are the groundwork, the Two Core Values are the beams and pillars, and the Goal is the building itself. So if someone memorises 321 as three slogans, they have misunderstood it: 321 is a set of building plans, and plans are meant to produce a house.

The fivefold change

321 says the fivefold change is in mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. A change of mindset — Babylon is not a place but a system; coming out is not moving house but switching to a different set of operating principles. A change of life — the person inside who says “I will build, I will make my name great” is gradually exchanged for the one who says “‘I’ no longer live, but Christ lives in me.” A change of daily living — this new life shows up in your mornings, your diary, your wallet. A change of relationships — you no longer fight to win in conflicts with your co-workers in ministry; you begin to be able to bow your head first. A change of ministry — God places his commission into the hands of a vessel that has already been built.

Brothers and sisters, remember the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

The 920 practice

321 says: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

Galatians 5:22–23: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” Notice that the Bible says “fruit,” singular; these nine are not nine elective courses but nine facets of one life. And fruit is not manufactured; it grows.

Brothers and sisters, this is how God’s system is established: not by my straining to look patient at the office, but by letting Christ live in me, so that patience flows out naturally.

The ultimate direction of the Goal

321 says that we establish God’s system in order to fulfil the Lord’s Prayer, to press on into the end time revival, and to walk alongside every person until they become an overcomer.

The heart of the Lord’s Prayer is Matthew 6:10: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” God’s system is the shape God’s will takes when it is done on earth: a family living by 321 is a small piece of the territory of God’s kingdom; a fellowship living by 321 is an outpost of the kingdom of heaven. And the final outcome has already been proclaimed in Revelation 11:15: “The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!”

sections.heading: 10. Putting It into Practice: How to Establish God’s System in Everyday Life
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very concrete exercises. Brothers and sisters, please take out a pen and write them down.

Exercise 1: Every morning, first settle on one “321 choice”

The lesson says to begin each morning by asking yourself three questions:

Today, am I willing to let Jesus be King, rather than deciding by myself?

Today, am I willing to let Jesus receive the glory, rather than seeking to make myself conspicuous?

Today, will I take the Bible as my standard, Jesus as my role model and the Holy Spirit as my guide?

The lesson says: “A declaration and resolution like this is the beginning of establishing God’s system.” Note the timing — you settle it “first”: before you look at your phone, before you open your email, before your children’s crying sweeps you into the rush of the day.

The Lord Jesus himself did exactly this. Mark 1:35: “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.” Psalm 5:3 also says: “Yahweh, in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.”

The first choice of the day sets the direction for all the other choices of the day. That is what our 321 Morning Devotion is about.

Exercise 2: In every small decision, choose 321 principles

The lesson lists three situations: when emotions rise, let the Holy Spirit guide me rather than letting my own will explode; when facing conflict with co-workers, let Jesus be King rather than fighting to win; when facing pressure and temptation, let the principles of the Bible decide how I respond, rather than acting on my feelings.

When emotions rise, James 1:19–20 says: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger; for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.” Be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slower still to anger.

In conflict with co-workers, Philippians 2:3 says: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself.” Letting Jesus be King means this: the outcome of this matter is not for me to decide, nor for the other person to decide; it is for the Lord to decide.

Under pressure and temptation, the Lord Jesus gave us the model when he was tempted in the wilderness. Matthew 4:4: “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.’” Three temptations, and three times the answer was “It is written.”

Exercise 3: Before each day ends, look back in your devotional time

The lesson says to ask three questions before each day ends:

At what moment did I not let Jesus be King?

Where did I seek my own glory?

In what matter did I depart from the Bible or ignore the prompting of the Holy Spirit?

And then the lesson adds this precious reminder: “Reflection is not condemnation, but repentance and renewal. To turn back is to build again.”

Psalm 139:23–24 is the best evening prayer: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” Notice that this prayer does not end with “Condemn me,” but with “lead me in the everlasting way.” The purpose of self-examination is guidance, not accusation.

Deepening the exercises with the eight stages of changing our mindset

321’s eight stages of changing our mindset are: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let’s place today’s exercises into these eight stages one by one.

1. Information: today you have already received it — Babylon is a system, and God’s system has to be established through every single choice.

2. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to turn information into revelation. Ephesians 1:17: “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him.” Stop and pray today: Lord, let me see which part of me is still living in Babylon.

3. Conviction: revelation that doesn’t lead to conviction is only being moved. Conviction says: I believe this is true, and I am willing to adjust my life accordingly.

4. Implementation: starting tomorrow morning, do Exercise 1 — the first thing after you get up is not your phone but those three questions.

5. Evaluation: every evening, do Exercise 3, and ask yourself at what moment today you made yourself king.

6. Correction: as soon as you find you’ve gone off course, turn back at once. Wrong? Then change — don’t put it off till next week.

7. Repetition: this is the most crucial step and the most unglamorous. The 2010 study by Lally’s team at University College London reminds us that it takes an average of sixty-six days for a behaviour to become automatic. Give yourself sixty-six days, not six.

8. Multiplication: when you begin to receive, go and find a “2” and pass on to them what you have received. 2 Timothy 2:2: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” There are four generations in this verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. That is multiplication; that is a system.

sections.heading: 11. Key Point 7: Habit Becomes a System, and the System Becomes Life
sections.html:
The lesson says: “The 321 life begins as training, then becomes habit, and finally becomes the natural overflow of life. As we choose again and again and practise again and again, 321 is no longer a framework but the very substance of our life.”

Brothers and sisters, look at these three stages: in the training stage it takes effort, and you have to remind yourself; in the habit stage it is natural, and you don’t need reminding; in the life stage it is joyful, and you wouldn’t want to do otherwise. A child learning the piano spends the first year counting beats and practising scales — that is training; by the third year the fingers move without thinking — that is habit; by the tenth year he sits down at the piano not to practise but because he loves it — that is life.

The lesson goes on: “God’s system is established bit by bit in our daily living. A life like this draws God’s presence and glory, and also draws people to Christ.” Matthew 5:16: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” What people see is the good works, but the one who receives the glory is the Father — and that is exactly the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

Psalm 1:2–3 describes this kind of life: “but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night. He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.”

A tree doesn’t strain to bear fruit; a tree only has to be planted by the streams of water. Brothers and sisters, where your roots go down determines what fruit you will bear.

sections.heading: 12. Closing and Call: Revival Begins with Each Day’s 321 Choice
sections.html:
The lesson’s closing words say: “The key to revival is not waiting for the right moment or a special conference, but beginning with each person’s 321 choices, every day.”

Brothers and sisters, we all long for revival, and we often think: when will it be our turn? Today the lesson gives an answer that pierces the heart: revival is not far away; revival is in the choice you made this morning.

The truly great revivals of history almost never began in a great auditorium. In August 1727 the Moravian Brethren at Herrnhut experienced an outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and soon afterwards began a round-the-clock prayer watch in shifts, day and night without ceasing, which lasted more than a hundred years. A hundred years of revival began with a group of people deciding to kneel down, every day, according to a rota.

Revival is not a firework; revival is a furnace. A firework needs lighting once; a furnace needs fuel added every day.

The lesson finally gives us a declaration, and I invite you, brothers and sisters, to say it with me from your heart:

“I will come out of Babylon; I will establish God’s system. I will let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive the glory, and let my life reflect the pattern of the kingdom of heaven!”

Brothers and sisters, will you begin to make this choice today? May we no longer use our own methods to build human kingdoms; may we return every day to the Three Foundations, hold fast to the Two Core Values and face towards that one Goal.

Because on that day, the Bible says (Revelation 21:3): “Behold, God’s dwelling is with people, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.” Babylon will fall; God’s system will endure forever. And today that everlasting building is being built, beginning with every tiny choice of yours and mine.

May all the glory be to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb, forever and ever. Amen.

keyVerses: “I heard another voice from heaven, saying, ‘Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues.’” (Revelation 18:4)
“Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans! With a voice of singing announce this, tell it even to the end of the earth: say, ‘Yahweh has redeemed his servant Jacob!’” (Isaiah 48:20)
