blog.title: Revival Is Not a Meeting; It Is a Heart Beating Again

blocks.x: Subtitle: Pressing on towards the End Time Revival — it begins with me
A man collapses in the street. His heart has stopped. A ring of people gathers round. Some film, some talk, some call an ambulance — but no one crouches down and presses their hands on his chest.

The American Heart Association points out that when cardiac arrest happens outside a hospital, if a bystander begins CPR straight away, the person’s chance of survival can double or even triple. The difference doesn’t lie with the man who fell. The difference lies with the people beside him — whether or not they are willing to kneel down.
That is the truest picture of “revival”.
The original meaning of revival is “to make alive again”

We are so used to picturing revival as a conference, a speaker, a song that moves us to tears. The meeting ends, the lights go out, the next day life carries on as before, and we say, “That was a wonderful weekend.”
But that isn’t revival — that’s being moved. Being moved is precious, but it passes. Revival doesn’t pass, because revival is the dead coming back to life.
The original word for “revival” means “to make alive again”. Paul says: “You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins” (Ephesians 2:1).

Ezekiel gives the clearest picture of all. God brought the prophet to a valley full of dry bones, and then: “the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army” (Ezekiel 37:10).

Notice the order: first they lived, then they stood up, and only last of all did they become an army. Life comes first, action follows, and ministry comes last. Dry bones can be arranged very neatly — but neat is not the same as alive.
From the Garden to the Throne, God’s Purpose Has Never Changed
In the beginning God said to humanity: “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it” (Genesis 1:28). Human beings were created to be kings entrusted with the stewardship of the whole earth.

But Satan said to them: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). The heart of the problem was never the fruit; it was “like God”. Humanity left its originally intended position, wanting to take God’s place, and its kingship collapsed.
So the road to restoration has to be the same road walked in reverse — give sovereignty back to God, and let Jesus be King.

The first Adam said, “I want to be like God.” The second Adam said in the garden of Gethsemane, “not what I desire, but what you desire.” He emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to the point of death — and then God highly exalted him.
The way down is the way up.

And this is where the hope of the End Time Revival lies. The Lord promises: “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne” (Revelation 3:21).
The word “as” matters a great deal. The way we reign must be just as the way Jesus reigns — through the cross, not through a scramble for power.
The Cost of Revival: Life as Its Firewood
Revival has never been free.

Stephen was stoned to death, yet before he died he asked forgiveness for the very people stoning him. He died, and the church came alive — from that day the disciples were scattered, and the gospel walked out of Jerusalem.

In the Rocky Mountains of North America there is a tree called the lodgepole pine. Its cones are sealed tightly with resin, and the seeds can’t get out. Only when a forest fire sweeps through and the heat melts the resin do the cones split open; then the seeds fall onto ground the fire has cleared, and a new forest grows.
Some seeds cannot be released except through fire.
So when God allows the fire to reach you, don’t think only of escape. Perhaps that is the very moment he means to open you up and release the seed inside you.
Four Small Things, Starting Tomorrow Morning
1. Let Jesus be King each day. When you open your eyes, before you scroll through your phone, say first: “Lord, this day is yours.”
2. Let Jesus receive the glory each day. Each time you finish something, say: “All the glory to you.”

3. Examine yourself once a week. This week, did I take Jesus as my role model, the Bible as my standard, and follow the guidance of the Holy Spirit? Did I let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive the glory?
4. Offer yourself. Pray every day: “Lord, I want to be a vessel of revival — please begin with me.”

Don’t underestimate these four small things. Research suggests it takes on average about sixty-six days for a new habit to become automatic. So don’t give up after three days just because you don’t feel anything.
Revival is not an unreachable dream, nor a movement waiting for someone else to start it. We don’t wait until we have power before God uses us; it’s when God uses us that we discover the power.
In that ring of people in the street, the one God is looking for is the person willing to crouch down.
Reflection Question
What are you still holding tightly in your hands right now — something you are not yet willing to let fall into the ground like that grain of wheat?

brief12.title: Cover
notes: Towards the End Time Revival
Entering God’s Original Intention and Glory
“Subdue it” — Genesis 1:28
“Sit down with me” — Revelation 3:21
Revival begins with me
Key points:
1. Greet the brothers and sisters and explain that this lesson walks five stretches of road: definition, core, hope, path and cost.
2. Two key verses: Genesis 1:28 (the original commission) and Revelation 3:21 (the final promise).
3. State the main thread of the lesson: revival is not an activity but the dead coming back to life; it begins not with others but with me.
4. Add Habakkuk 3:2, “Renew your work in the middle of the years,” as the prayer for the whole lesson.

brief12.title: Introduction
notes: A heart that has stopped
A man collapses; a crowd looks on
Bystander CPR can double or
triple survival (American Heart Association)
The difference: who is willing to kneel
Key points:
1. Open with the scene of a man collapsing in the street — people watching, but no one crouching down.
2. Data: the American Heart Association points out that immediate bystander CPR can double or triple survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
3. Turn: the world is not about to fall ill — it has already collapsed; God is looking for people willing to kneel down.
4. Pose three questions: if revival came today, what must change at once? When did I last truly hand over sovereignty? Am I waiting for revival, or standing in its way?

brief12.title: Key Verses and Background
notes: From the garden to the throne
Genesis 1:28: God tells humanity to subdue the earth
Leaving our position, we lost our kingship
Revelation 3:21: the promise of sharing his throne
God’s purpose has never changed
Key points:
1. Genesis came from Moses; its first readers were the Israelites just out of Egypt after four hundred years of slavery — what they most lacked was an identity as kings.
2. Original: “subdue,” kabash (bring into order); “have dominion,” radah (reign). Humanity reigns as God’s image — an entrusted kingship.
3. Genesis 3:5, “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” — leaving our originally intended position is the fall; Cain killing Abel in Genesis 4:8 is the first result.
4. Revelation was written around AD 95 by John on Patmos; 3:21 comes from the letter to Laodicea, and 3:17 says they “don’t know that you are the wretched one, miserable, poor, blind, and naked.”
5. Conclusion: from Genesis 1:28 to Revelation 3:21, God wanted humanity to reign in the beginning, and still wants it at the end.

brief12.title: Key Point 1
notes: Revival: life restored out of death
“Revival” originally means: to make alive again
Ephesians 2:1: “You were made alive”
Ezekiel 37:10: the bones lived and stood up
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
Key points:
1. Original: Hebrew chayah in the Piel stem (intensive, factitive) = “to make alive”; see Psalm 85:6 and Habakkuk 3:2.
2. Ephesians 2:1 and 2:4–5, “made us alive together with Christ”; Luke 15:24, the prodigal “was dead, and is alive again.”
3. The order of the dry bones’ revival in Ezekiel 37: first they lived, then stood up, finally became an exceedingly great army — life first, then relationships, then ministry.
4. Warning: Revelation 3:1, “you have a reputation of being alive, but you are dead”; liveliness is not revival, growth is not revival.

5. Science: Jonas Frisén’s team at the Karolinska Institute, 2005, Cell — carbon-14 research confirming the body’s cells are continually renewed; compare 2 Corinthians 4:16, “our inward man is renewed day by day.”

brief12.title: Key Point 2
notes: Restoring the glory and calling we lost
Romans 3:23: we fall short of the glory of God
Eve’s failure: wanting to be God herself
Give sovereignty back; let Jesus be King
Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan
Key points:
1. “Fall short,” Greek hystereō = fail to reach, lag behind; the prince’s royal blood hasn’t changed, but his life looks nothing like a prince’s.
2. The first Adam said, “I want to be like God”; the second Adam said, “not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39).
3. Philippians 2:5–8, “emptied himself,” kenoō = to empty oneself out; the way down is the way up (2:9, God highly exalted him).
4. Illustration: two goats butting heads on a single-log bridge both fall in — pride provokes pride, and both sides lose.
5. Psychology: Carol Dweck of Stanford on fixed and growth mindsets, confirming that “someone who must protect his image cannot learn.”

brief12.title: Key Point 3
notes: Victors reign with Christ
Revelation 3:21: sit down with me on my throne
Overcoming: the Lamb’s blood, the word of testimony
Follow the Lord first, then fish for people
Revival spreads through relationships, not venues
Key points:
1. “As I also overcame” — our way of reigning must be “as” Jesus’: through the cross.
2. Revelation 5:10, “we will reign on the earth”; 11:15, “The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ.”
3. What overcoming consists of: Revelation 12:11 — the Lamb’s blood, the word of testimony, not loving their life.
4. Matthew 4:19: first “come after me,” then “fishers for men”; life first, then relationships, then ministry.

5. History: Acts 17:6, “These who have turned the world upside down have come here also”; the sociologist Rodney Stark, The Rise of Christianity (1996), shows the early church grew through households and relationships — echoing the 321 235 relationships.

brief12.title: Key Point 4
notes: From the inside out, to the ends of the earth
Acts 1:8: from Jerusalem to the uttermost parts
First the inside, then the outside
Mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry
First God, then ourselves, then others
Key points:
1. Acts 1:8 is the road map of revival, but its precondition is “when the Holy Spirit has come upon you.”
2. Proverbs 4:23, “out of it is the wellspring of life”; Romans 12:2, “transformed by the renewing of your mind,” metamorphoō = the change from caterpillar to butterfly.
3. The 321 fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry; the priority of relationships: first God, then ourselves, then others, finally things.
4. Illustration: a tree’s roots spread far wider than its crown; what keeps it standing lies below ground, not above.
5. History: the Welsh Revival of 1904–1905 (Evan Roberts) — pubs emptied, court cases dropped; the Pyongyang Revival in Korea in 1907 began with confession and reconciliation.

brief12.title: Key Point 5
notes: Not a slogan, but a life
John 12:24: the grain must die to bear fruit
Stephen’s martyrdom sent the gospel out of Jerusalem
Acts 20:24: not holding his life dear
Lodgepole cones open only in fire
Key points:
1. John 12:24, a grain of wheat; Romans 12:1, “present your bodies a living sacrifice” — the trouble is that a living sacrifice keeps crawling off the altar.
2. Stephen: Acts 7:59–60, then 8:1 the great persecution and 8:4, “those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word.”
3. Paul: Acts 20:24, “nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race.”
4. Scientific illustration: the serotinous cones of the North American lodgepole pine open only when heat melts the resin — some seeds cannot be released except through fire.

5. A famous saying: Henry Varley is generally believed to have told Moody, “The world has yet to see what God can do with a man fully consecrated to him”; Angela Duckworth’s 2007 research on grit confirms that persistence beats talent.

brief12.title: Integrating the 3-2-1 Vision
notes: 321 and revival
Three Foundations: role model, standard, guide
Two Core Values: King, and the glory
The Goal: establish God’s system
The 920 practice, the 235 relationships
Key points:

1. The Three Foundations in this lesson: Jesus is my role model (the self-emptying road of Philippians 2), the Bible is my standard (Habakkuk asked for the revival of your work), the Holy Spirit is my guide (Acts 1:8).
2. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King settles “who is in charge”; let Jesus receive the glory settles “who we do it for.”
3. The Goal: revival is not passing enthusiasm but the re-establishing of God’s system, for ever.
4. A shift in perspective: from man’s to God’s, earthly to heavenly, temporary to eternal, worldly to godly.

5. The 920 practice: before every “2,” live out the selfless “0” and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23); the 235 relationships: 2 companions, 3 spiritual parents and children, 5 a fivefold-ministry team.

brief12.title: Putting It into Practice
notes: Four daily practices
Let Jesus be King each day
Let Jesus receive the glory each day
Examine the 321 actions weekly
Offer yourself as a vessel of revival
Key points:
1. Practice 1: the first thing on waking, hand over sovereignty for the day; when facing difficulties, choose to obey God’s word rather than acting in the flesh.
2. Practice 2: each time you finish something, say “All the glory to you”; don’t promote yourself; learn to step back out of sight. Cite 1 Corinthians 10:31 and John 3:30.
3. Practice 3: examine the Three Foundations and Two Core Values weekly; if you drift, repent at once and choose again. Cite Psalm 139:23–24.
4. Practice 4: pray daily, “Lord, I want to be a vessel of revival — please begin with me.” Cite 2 Corinthians 4:7 and Jeremiah 18:4.

5. Deepen with the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Add Phillippa Lally’s 2010 research (about 66 days on average to form a habit) to encourage people not to give up after three days.

brief12.title: Closing and Call
notes: Revival begins with me
Not waiting, but becoming
Isaiah 60:1: Arise, shine!
Not spectators, but firewood
Lord, please begin with me
Key points:
1. Echo the introduction: God is looking for the one person willing to crouch down.
2. Three examples: Habakkuk praying as his nation was about to fall; Stephen kneeling to ask forgiveness for his enemies; Moody saying, “I will be that man.”
3. Key line: we don’t wait until we have power before God uses us; it’s when God uses us that we discover the power.
4. A concrete call: let Jesus reign over our schedule, wallet, marriage, temper and ambitions.
5. Close with Isaiah 60:1 and Habakkuk 2:14.

brief12.title: Response Prayer and Blessing
notes: Response prayer
Lord, I want to be a vessel of revival
Begin with me; kindle the fire of revival
Your Kingdom come, your will be done
on earth as it is in heaven
Key points:
1. Lead the brothers and sisters in praying together line by line, slowly.
2. The prayer includes three handings-back: of sovereignty, of glory, of ourselves.
3. Close with the words of the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:10).
4. Blessing: may the fire of revival be kindled in each one of us, and may Jesus reign among us and receive all the glory.

1. “Fall short,” Greek hystereō = fail to reach, lack, lag behind; not cancelled, but out of reach.
2. Illustration: a prince wandering homeless in the streets — royal blood unchanged, a life nothing like a prince’s.
3. The point of Genesis 3:5 is not the fruit but “like God” — the root of the problem is pride.

4. The 321 definition: pride is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position.
5. James 4:6, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

brief21.title: Key Point 2b
notes: The way down is the way up
Philippians 2:7: he emptied himself, a servant
kenoō: to empty oneself out
Philippians 2:9: God highly exalted him
Humility overcomes pride; both sides win
Key points:
1. The first Adam said, “I want to be like God”; the second Adam said in Gethsemane, “not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39).
2. The full path of Philippians 2:5–8: emptying himself, taking the form of a servant, humbling himself, obedient to the point of death.
3. “Emptied himself,” kenoō = to empty oneself out; not losing his divinity, but laying down his right to use it.
4. Illustration: two goats butting heads on a single-log bridge both fall in — pride provokes pride, and both sides lose.
5. Psychology: Carol Dweck of Stanford on fixed and growth mindsets, confirming that someone who must protect his self-image cannot learn.

brief21.title: Key Point 3a
notes: Sitting with the Lord on his throne
Revelation 3:21: as I also overcame
Revelation 5:10: we will reign on the earth
Revelation 11:15: the world’s kingdom becomes the Lord’s
Practise reigning from today
Key points:
1. Read Revelation 3:21 in full again, stressing “as” — our way of reigning must be as Jesus’ way of reigning.
2. Jesus didn’t overcome with the sword; he overcame on the cross.
3. Revelation 5:10, “we will reign on the earth” — not waiting until heaven.
4. Revelation 11:15 is the final outcome: the kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ.
5. 321 application: reigning isn’t controlling others but governing yourself; not subduing your circumstances, but refusing to be subdued by yourself in them.

brief21.title: Key Point 3b
notes: What is overcoming?
Revelation 12:11: because of the Lamb’s blood
and the word of their testimony
They didn’t love their life, even to death
Victors are ordinary people who handed over sovereignty
Key points:
1. “Overcome,” Greek nikaō; its content is in Revelation 12:11.
2. Three things: the Lamb’s blood (not my goodness), the word of their testimony (not my eloquence), not loving their life (not my holding back).
3. Victors are not spiritual supermen, but ordinary people who have handed over sovereignty, given away the glory and laid down their lives.
4. Examples: the moment you’re about to lose your temper; the moment you’re misunderstood and long to explain; the moment you’ve achieved something and long to be noticed.

brief21.title: Key Point 3c
notes: Fishers for men
Matthew 4:19: fishers for men
Follow first, then win people
Acts 17:6: those who turned the world upside down
Revival spreads through relationships: the 235
Key points:
1. Matthew 4:19: first “come after me,” then “fishers for men”; the order cannot be reversed.
2. Reminder: someone who isn’t following the Lord brings back his own followers, not disciples of Christ.
3. Acts 17:6: a group with no status, resources or army was regarded as a force turning the world upside down.
4. The sociologist Rodney Stark, The Rise of Christianity (1996): the early church grew through households, relationships and self-denying care for the sick in plagues, not large gatherings.
5. 321 application: the 235 relationships — 2 spiritual companions, 3 spiritual parents and children, 5 a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

brief21.title: Key Point 4a
notes: The inside-out road map
Acts 1:8: the Spirit comes, to the ends of the earth
First the inside, then the outside
Proverbs 4:23: the wellspring of life is the heart
Mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry
Key points:
1. Acts 1:8 is the road map of revival: Jerusalem, all Judea, Samaria, to the uttermost parts of the earth — spreading outward ring by ring.
2. But its precondition is “when the Holy Spirit has come upon you” — first power, then witness.
3. Proverbs 4:23, “out of it is the wellspring of life”; God doesn’t change the circumstances first; he changes the person first.
4. The 321 fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry; the priority of relationships: first God, then ourselves, then others, finally things.
5. Illustration: a tree’s roots spread far wider than its crown; whether it stands in the wind depends on what is below ground.

brief21.title: Key Point 4b
notes: Revival shakes society
Romans 12:2: transformed by the renewing of your mind
metamorphoō: caterpillar to butterfly
Wales 1904: the pubs emptied
Pyongyang 1907: began with confession and reconciliation
Key points:
1. “Transformed” in Romans 12:2, metamorphoō = to change form, the same word used of the Lord’s transfiguration (Matthew 17:2).
2. Not painting the caterpillar a new colour, but remaking it entirely from the inside.
3. The Welsh Revival of 1904–1905, led by Evan Roberts; accounts tell of pubs emptied, court cases dropping, even pit ponies unable for a while to understand commands given without swearing.
4. The Pyongyang Revival of 1907 in Korea began with public confession and reconciliation, and deeply shaped the Korean church’s tradition of prayer.
5. Conclusion: no one launched a social reform; hearts changed and society changed. Revival is lasting change, not a chance event.

brief21.title: Key Point 5a
notes: The lesson of a grain of wheat
John 12:24: falls into the earth and dies
and bears much fruit
Romans 12:1: present your bodies a living sacrifice
Offering is not once, but every day
Key points:
1. John 12:24: a grain kept is safe — but it will always be just one grain.
2. The arithmetic of revival is the reverse of the world’s: hold on and you lose; let go and you gain.
3. Romans 12:1, “present your bodies a living sacrifice”; the trouble with a living sacrifice is that it keeps crawling off the altar, so it must be offered every day.
4. 321 application: selflessness overcomes Satan — what Satan fears most is not the gifted Christian but the Christian with no “self” left.

brief21.title: Key Point 5b
notes: Three testimonies of revival
Stephen martyred; the disciples scattered and preached
Acts 8:4: they went around preaching the word
Acts 20:24: that I may finish my race
The disciples opened revival’s history with their blood
Key points:
1. Stephen: Acts 7:59–60, he asked forgiveness for those stoning him; 8:1 the great persecution and the disciples scattered; 8:4, “those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word.”
2. He died, and the church came alive — one grain of wheat fell into the ground, and the gospel walked out of Jerusalem.
3. Paul: Acts 20:24, “nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race.”
4. The apostles: according to church tradition, apart from John most were martyred; they left no buildings, yet opened the history of revival with their blood.

brief21.title: Key Point 5c
notes: Released only through fire
Lodgepole cones sealed with resin
Only after a fire are the seeds released
Torn down to carry a greater glory
Not playing at faith, but staking our lives on our trust
Key points:
1. Science: the serotinous cones of the North American lodgepole pine open only when heat melts the resin; the seeds fall on ground cleared by fire and grow into a new forest.
2. Application: when God allows the fire to reach you, don’t think only of escape; it may be the very moment he releases the seed within you.
3. A famous saying: Henry Varley is generally believed to have told Moody, “The world has yet to see what God can do with a man fully consecrated to him.” Moody decided to be that man.
4. Psychology: Angela Duckworth (University of Pennsylvania, 2007, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology) on grit — long-term achievement depends on perseverance, not talent.
5. The lesson’s question: are we willing to lay down everything for the kingdom of God, holding nothing back?

brief21.title: Putting It into Practice (1)
notes: Practices 1 and 2
Let Jesus be King each day
On waking, hand over the day’s sovereignty
Let Jesus receive the glory each day
In everything say: the glory to you
Key points:
1. Practice 1: the first thing on waking, pray and hand over the day’s sovereignty; when facing difficulties, choose to obey God’s word rather than acting in the flesh. Cite Romans 11:36.
2. Practice 2: each time you finish something, say “All the glory to you”; don’t promote yourself, don’t compete for applause, learn to step back out of sight. Cite 1 Corinthians 10:31 and John 3:30.
3. Model the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

4. Research: Emmons and McCullough (2003, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology) found that people who regularly recorded gratitude had markedly higher well-being — giving glory needs repetition.

brief21.title: Putting It into Practice (2)
notes: Practices 3 and 4
Weekly, examine the Three Foundations and Two Core Values
If you drift, repent at once and choose again
Offer yourself as a vessel of revival
Pray: Lord, please begin with me
Key points:
1. Practice 3: at a set time each week, examine the Three Foundations and Two Core Values; write down six questions and change only the weakest. Cite Psalm 139:23–24.
2. Practice 4: pray daily, “Lord, I want to be a vessel of revival — please begin with me”; be willing to be torn down and built up. Cite 2 Corinthians 4:7 and Jeremiah 18:4.
3. Repetition: Phillippa Lally (University College London, 2010) found that a new habit takes on average about 66 days to become automatic — don’t give up after three days.
4. Multiplication: do it with one other person and that’s the “2”; bring someone along and that’s the “3”.

brief21.title: Summing Up the 3-2-1 Vision
notes: Summing up the 3-2-1 vision
Three Foundations: role model, standard, guide
Two Core Values: King, and the glory
The Goal: establish God’s system
The self-centred life is death; selflessness is life
Key points:
1. The Three Foundations in this lesson: Jesus is my role model (Philippians 2), the Bible is my standard (Habakkuk asked for the revival of your work), the Holy Spirit is my guide (Acts 1:8).
2. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King settles “who is in charge”; let Jesus receive the glory settles “who we do it for.”
3. The Goal: revival is not passing enthusiasm but the re-establishing of God’s system, for ever.
4. Galatians 2:20, “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” — selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the boundlessness of Christ.
5. The shift in perspective, the 920 practice and the 235 relationships; the Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: Revival begins with me
Not waiting, but becoming
Isaiah 60:1: Arise, shine!
Habakkuk 2:14: the earth filled with his glory
Not spectators, but firewood
Key points:
1. Echo the introduction: God is looking for the one person willing to crouch down.
2. Three examples: Habakkuk praying as his nation was about to fall; Stephen kneeling to ask forgiveness for his enemies; Moody saying, “I will be that man.”
3. Key line: we don’t wait until we have power before God uses us; it’s when God uses us that we discover the power.
4. A concrete call: let Jesus reign over our schedule, wallet, marriage, temper and ambitions; take one step back, and he shows a little more.
5. Cite Isaiah 60:1 and Habakkuk 2:14, and point with Philippians 2:10–11 to every knee bowing and every tongue confessing.

brief21.title: Response Prayer and Blessing
notes: Response prayer and blessing
Lord, I want to be a vessel of revival
Begin with me; kindle the fire of revival
Your Kingdom come, your will be done
on earth as it is in heaven
Key points:
1. Lead the brothers and sisters in praying together line by line, slowly, leaving space for the Holy Spirit to work.
2. Three handings-back: of sovereignty, of glory, of ourselves.
3. Include confession: we often treat revival as an event yet refuse to pay the price with our lives; we envy others’ branches and leaves yet won’t put down roots.
4. Close with the words of the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:10).
5. Blessing: may the fire of revival be kindled in each one of us, and may Jesus reign among us and receive all the glory.

script12.title: Cover
script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come to Lesson 8: Towards the End Time Revival. We have two key verses today. In Genesis 1:28 God says to humanity: “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it.” In Revelation 3:21 the Lord Jesus says: “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne.” One is at the beginning, the other at the end. The great stretch in between is the road we will walk today.

script12.title: Introduction
script: Picture a scene. A man suddenly collapses in the street. His heart has stopped. A ring of people gathers round. Some film, some talk — but no one crouches down and presses their hands on his chest. The American Heart Association points out that when cardiac arrest happens outside a hospital, if a bystander begins CPR straight away, the chance of survival can double or even triple. Brothers and sisters, the difference doesn’t lie with the man who fell. The difference lies with the people beside him — whether or not they are willing to kneel down.

script12.title: Key Verses and Background
script: Genesis came from the hand of Moses, and its first readers were the Israelites, just out of Egypt after four hundred years of slavery. The word “reign” had no place in a slave’s mindset. So God said: you were always meant to be kings entrusted with the stewardship of the whole earth. But Satan said: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” He didn’t urge them to break a rule; he urged them to change places — not to be the king God had appointed, but to be their own god. Yet by Revelation, the Lord still says: I will give him to sit down with me. God’s purpose has never changed.

script12.title: Key Point 1: The Definition of Revival
script: What is revival? The original word means “to make alive again.” Paul says: “You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins.” In Ezekiel 37, God brought the prophet to a valley of dry bones. And what happened? “They lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army.” Notice the order: first they lived, then they stood up, and only last did they become an army. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Brothers and sisters, liveliness is not revival, growth is not revival, and being moved is not revival either.

script12.title: Key Point 2: The Core of Revival
script: What did humanity lose? “For all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God.” How did humanity fall? Eve’s failure was wanting to be God herself. So the road to restoration has to be the same road walked in reverse — give sovereignty back to God, and let Jesus be King. The first Adam said, “I want to be like God.” The second Adam said in the garden of Gethsemane, “not what I desire, but what you desire.” The way down is the way up. Two goats butted heads on a single-log bridge, and both fell into the river. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

script12.title: Key Point 3: The Hope of Revival
script: The Lord says: “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame.” Notice the word “as.” Jesus didn’t overcome with the sword; he overcame on the cross. What is overcoming? Revelation 12:11 says: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.” The Lord also says: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers for men.” Follow first, then win people. Brothers and sisters, reigning isn’t controlling others; reigning is governing yourself.

script12.title: Key Point 4: The Path of Revival
script: Before he ascended, the Lord said: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” These are concentric circles spreading outward ring by ring. But the very first clause is: when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. First the inside, then the outside. 321 says the change is fivefold: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. In the Welsh Revival of 1904, nobody launched a social reform movement. People’s hearts changed — and the pubs emptied and the court cases dropped.

script12.title: Key Point 5: The Cost of Revival
script: Revival has never been free. The fire of revival is lit with life as its firewood. The Lord says: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” Stephen was stoned to death, but from that day the disciples were scattered, and the gospel walked out of Jerusalem. Paul says: “nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race.” In North America there is a pine whose cones are sealed with resin; only when a great fire sweeps through are the seeds released. Some seeds cannot be released except through fire.

script12.title: Integrating the 3-2-1 Vision
script: Let’s set this lesson within 321 and look at it once more. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — as he overcame, so we overcome; the Bible is my standard — being moved can deceive us, the Bible will not; the Holy Spirit is my guide — our responsibility is not to make the fire but to prepare the firewood. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King settles who is in charge; let Jesus receive the glory settles who we do it for. The Goal: establish God’s system.

script12.title: Putting It into Practice
script: The lesson gives four practices. First, resolve each day to let Jesus be King. Tomorrow morning, when you open your eyes, before you scroll through your phone, say first: “Lord, today is yours.” Second, let Jesus receive the glory each day. Each time you finish something, say: “All the glory to you.” Third, examine your 321 actions weekly: have I lived out the Three Foundations? Have I practised the Two Core Values? If I’ve drifted, repent at once. Fourth, offer yourself as a vessel of revival. Research suggests it takes on average sixty-six days to form a new habit, so don’t give up after three days.

script12.title: Closing and Call
script: Brothers and sisters, revival is not an unreachable dream, nor a movement waiting for someone else to start it. Revival begins with the 321 choices you and I make every day. Let’s go back to that scene in the street: a ring of people stands watching, and the one God is looking for is the person willing to crouch down. We don’t wait until we have power before God uses us; it’s when God uses us that we discover the power. Isaiah 60:1 says: “Arise, shine; for your light has come.” Not spectators, but firewood.

script12.title: Response Prayer and Blessing
script: Let’s pray together. Lord Jesus, you are the God who raises the dead. We confess that we often treat revival as an event, yet refuse to pay the price with our lives. Please forgive us. Today we hand our sovereignty back to you, we hand the glory back to you, and we hand ourselves back to you. Lord, I want to be a vessel of revival — please begin with me. Your Kingdom come, your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

script21.title: Cover
script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come to Lesson 8: Towards the End Time Revival, subtitled Entering God’s Original Intention and Glory. We have two key verses today. Genesis 1:28: “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it.” Revelation 3:21: “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame.” One is at the beginning, the other at the end. Today we will walk five stretches of road: the definition of revival, its core, its hope, its path and its cost. Revival is not a topic; revival is a decision.

script21.title: Introduction (1)
script: Picture a scene. A man suddenly collapses in the street. His heart has stopped. A ring of people gathers round. Some film, some talk — but no one crouches down and presses their hands on his chest. The American Heart Association points out that when cardiac arrest happens outside a hospital, if a bystander begins CPR straight away, the chance of survival can double or even triple. The principle of CPR is very simple: hands on the outside take the place of the heart that has stopped, pushing the blood out. The rescuer cannot create life; he only keeps the channel open. Brothers and sisters, that is our place in revival.

script21.title: Introduction (2)
script: I want to ask you three questions. Please answer them honestly. First: if God brought down the fire of revival on you today, what one thing in your life would have to change immediately? Second: when was the last time you truly said, “Lord, you be in charge of this”? Third: are you waiting for revival, or standing in its way? We often picture revival as a conference, a speaker, a song. The meeting ends, the lights go out, and life carries on as before. Brothers and sisters, that isn’t revival — that’s being moved. Being moved passes; revival doesn’t, because revival is the dead coming back to life.

script21.title: Key Verses and Background
script: First, the background. Genesis came from the hand of Moses, and its first readers were the Israelites, just out of Egypt after four hundred years of slavery. The word “reign” had no place in a slave’s mindset. The original is fascinating: “subdue it” means to bring into order; “have dominion over the fish of the sea” means to reign, to rule. But this is an entrusted kingship — humanity reigns as the image of God, and a mirror turned away from the light reflects nothing at all. Now Revelation. The apostle John was exiled on the island of Patmos around AD 95. Our key verse comes from the letter to the church in Laodicea. Laodicea was very wealthy, yet the Lord said: you don’t know that you are the wretched one, miserable, poor, blind, and naked. Brothers and sisters, Laodicea was not a church short of money; it was a church short of life.

script21.title: Key Point 1a
script: What is revival? The original word means “to make alive again.” Psalm 85:6 says: “Won’t you revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?” Paul says: “You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins.” The phrase “made alive together” in Ephesians is, in Greek, a compound Paul coined himself, because the words that already existed weren’t enough. The Lord himself told the story: when the prodigal came home, his father said, “this, my son, was dead, and is alive again.” The son’s body had been alive the whole time, yet his father said he had been dead. So in God’s eyes, living inside yourself is death.

script21.title: Key Point 1b
script: The clearest picture is in Ezekiel. God brought the prophet to a valley of dry bones and asked him: Can these bones live? Then he said: I will cause breath to enter into you, and you will live. And the result: “they lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army.” Notice the order: first they lived, then they stood up, and only last did they become an army. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Some say, “Our church is full every week.” But brothers and sisters, dry bones can be arranged very neatly, and neat is not the same as alive. The Lord said to the church in Sardis: “you have a reputation of being alive, but you are dead.” Liveliness is not revival; growth is not revival.

script21.title: Key Point 2a
script: Next, the core of revival. What did humanity lose? Paul says it all in one sentence: “for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God.” “Fall short” means to fail to reach, to be out of reach. It’s like a prince wandering homeless in the streets: his royal blood hasn’t changed, but his life looks nothing like a prince’s. How did humanity fall? The serpent said: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” The heart of the problem isn’t the fruit; it’s “like God.” Brothers and sisters, that is pride: leaving our originally intended position, grasping power, wanting to take God’s place. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

script21.title: Key Point 2b
script: The first Adam said, “I want to be like God.” The second Adam said in the garden of Gethsemane, “not what I desire, but what you desire.” Paul writes it very clearly: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” To empty himself means to pour himself out. Jesus didn’t lose his divinity; he laid down his right to use it. And then? God highly exalted him. The way down is the way up. Two goats met on a single-log bridge; neither would back down, they locked horns, and both fell into the river. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

script21.title: Key Point 3a
script: The third stretch is the hope of revival. The Lord says: “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame.” Notice the word “as.” Jesus didn’t overcome with the sword; he overcame on the cross. So our road to sitting with him on his throne must also pass through obedience and the denying of self. Revelation 5:10 says: “we will reign on the earth.” Notice: on the earth — not starting only once we get to heaven. And the final outcome is already written: the kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. Brothers and sisters, reigning isn’t controlling others; reigning is governing yourself.

script21.title: Key Point 3b
script: What is overcoming? Revelation 12:11 says: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.” Three things: the blood of the Lamb — not my goodness; the word of their testimony — not my eloquence; not loving their life — not my holding back. So overcomers are not spiritual supermen; they are ordinary people who have handed over their sovereignty and given away the glory. The moment you’re about to lose your temper, let Jesus be King — and you have overcome. The moment you long to be noticed, let Jesus receive the glory — and you have overcome.

script21.title: Key Point 3c
script: The lesson reminds us: when we learn to be fishers for men, no longer promoting ourselves but proclaiming Jesus, we are already entering revival. The Lord said: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers for men.” Follow first, then win people. When someone who isn’t following the Lord goes out to win people, all he brings back are followers of himself. The early church swept across the Roman Empire. Acts 17:6 records the cry: “These who have turned the world upside down have come here also.” The sociologist Rodney Stark points out that the early church grew not through large gatherings but through households, relationships and self-denying care for the sick during plagues. Brothers and sisters, revival spreads through relationships. That is exactly the 235 relationships of 321.

script21.title: Key Point 4a
script: The fourth stretch is the path of revival. Before he ascended, the Lord said: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” These are concentric circles spreading outward ring by ring. But the very first clause is: when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. First the inside, then the outside. Proverbs 4:23 says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” 321 says the change is fivefold: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Many people want to start from step five and go straight to doing great ministry — and end up building their house on sand.

script21.title: Key Point 4b
script: Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” In Greek this “transformed” is metamorphosis — the change by which a caterpillar becomes a butterfly. It isn’t painting the caterpillar a new colour; it’s remaking it entirely from the inside. And change like this always shakes the outside. The Welsh Revival of 1904–1905 was led by a young man, Evan Roberts. Those who came to the Lord numbered in the tens of thousands, and even more striking were the changes in society: the pubs lost their trade, court cases dropped, and there are even accounts that the miners stopped swearing, so that for a while the ponies hauling the coal couldn’t understand their new commands. The Pyongyang Revival in Korea in 1907 likewise began with public confession of sin and reconciliation with one another. Brothers and sisters, when hearts change, society changes.

script21.title: Key Point 5a
script: The last stretch is the cost of revival. Revival has never been free; the fire of revival is lit with life as its firewood. The Lord says: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” Keep a grain of wheat and it’s safe — but it will always be just one grain. The arithmetic of revival is the reverse of the world’s: hold on and you lose; let go and you gain. Paul says: “present your bodies a living sacrifice.” The phrase itself carries a tension — a sacrifice is supposed to be dead, but a living sacrifice has to go on being offered while it lives. As someone has well said, the biggest problem with a living sacrifice is that it keeps crawling off the altar.

script21.title: Key Point 5b
script: The lesson gives three testimonies. The first is Stephen. As they stoned him, he kneeled down and cried, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” He died, and the church came alive. From that day the disciples were scattered, and the Bible says: “those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word.” One grain of wheat fell into the ground, and the gospel walked out of Jerusalem. The second is Paul. In Acts 20:24 he says: “nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race.” The third is the apostles as a whole. According to church tradition, apart from John most of the Lord’s disciples were martyred. They left behind no buildings, yet with their blood they opened the history of revival.

script21.title: Key Point 5c
script: Let me share a scientific fact. In the Rocky Mountains of North America there is a pine whose cones are coated in resin and normally stay tightly shut, so the seeds can’t get out. Only when a forest fire sweeps through and the heat melts the resin do the cones split open; the seeds fall on ground the fire has cleared, and a new forest grows. Brothers and sisters, some seeds cannot be released except through fire. So when God allows the fire to reach you, don’t think only of escape. As a young man Moody heard a sentence, generally believed to have been spoken to him by Henry Varley: “The world has yet to see what God can do with a man fully consecrated to him.” Moody said: I will be that man. What Satan fears most is not the gifted Christian; it’s the Christian who has no “self” left.

script21.title: Putting It into Practice (1)
script: The lesson gives four practices. First, resolve each day to let Jesus be King. Tomorrow morning, when you open your eyes, before you scroll through your phone, say first: “Lord, this day is yours. My time, my emotions, my decisions — I hand them all to you.” When you face difficulties, choose to obey God’s word rather than acting in the flesh. Second, let Jesus receive the glory each day. Each time you finish something, say out loud: “All the glory to you.” In a 2003 study the psychologists Emmons and McCullough found that people who regularly recorded their gratitude had markedly higher well-being. Thanksgiving needs repetition, and so does giving glory.

script21.title: Putting It into Practice (2)
script: Third, practise the 321 actions at a set time each week. Find a quiet time and ask yourself six questions: This week, did I take Jesus as my role model? Did I take the Bible as my standard? Did I follow the guidance of the Holy Spirit? Did I let Jesus be King? Did I let Jesus receive the glory? Am I establishing God’s system, or my own? Whichever is weakest, change only that one. Fourth, offer yourself as a vessel of revival, and pray every day: “Lord, please begin with me.” Research suggests that a new habit takes on average about sixty-six days to become automatic, so don’t give up after three days.

script21.title: Summing Up the 3-2-1 Vision
script: Let’s set this lesson within 321 and look at it once more. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — as he overcame, so we overcome; the Bible is my standard — being moved can deceive us, numbers can deceive us, the Bible will not; the Holy Spirit is my guide — our responsibility is not to make the fire but to prepare the firewood. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King settles who is in charge; let Jesus receive the glory settles who we do it for. The Goal: establish God’s system. Paul says: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Selflessness is not wiping yourself out; it is stepping out of that small, cramped self and entering into the boundlessness of Christ.

script21.title: Closing and Call
script: Brothers and sisters, revival is not an unreachable dream, nor a movement waiting for someone else to start it. Revival begins with the 321 choices you and I make every day. Let’s go back to that scene in the street: a ring of people stands watching, and the one God is looking for is the person willing to crouch down. One Habakkuk, as his nation was about to fall, praying, “Renew your work in the middle of the years.” One Stephen, kneeling down to ask forgiveness for the people stoning him. God is still asking the same question today: whom can I begin with? We don’t wait until we have power before God uses us; it’s when God uses us that we discover the power. Isaiah says: “Arise, shine; for your light has come.” Not spectators, but firewood.

script21.title: Response Prayer and Blessing
script: Let’s bow our heads and pray together. Lord Jesus, you are the God who raises the dead. We confess that we often treat revival as an event, yet refuse to pay the price with our lives; we envy other people’s branches and leaves, yet won’t let you put down roots in us. Please forgive us. Today we hand our sovereignty back to you, and we hand the glory back to you as well; take away our longing to be seen, so that people see only Jesus. Lord, I want to be a vessel of revival — please begin with me. Your Kingdom come, your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

sections.heading: Introduction: One Well, Three Rings
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. May the peace of the Lord come upon you this early morning.

Let me begin with a question: if God were to start working in you today, where would you want him to begin?

Most of us would answer — with my circumstances. Lord, change my job, change my family, change our church. But the order the Bible shows us is exactly the reverse. God never begins by changing circumstances; he begins by changing people. And he doesn’t begin by changing a crowd; he begins by changing one person.

Let me tell you a true story.

In 1727, in a little place in eastern Germany called Herrnhut, there lived a band of believers who had come there as refugees. They came from different countries, different denominations, different languages, and persecution for their faith had gathered them onto the estate of Count Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf (1700–1760). Put enough people together and trouble comes. They criticised one another, condemned one another, argued endlessly over whose theology was orthodox, and the whole village was on the verge of splitting apart.

On 12 May that year, Zinzendorf went from house to house and led the whole village to sign a “Brotherly Agreement”, a covenant with one another: to lay down their rivalry, to love one another, and to serve with one heart. On 13 August they took Communion together. And on that very day, the Holy Spirit was poured out. No one could describe what happened in that moment. All they knew was that the walls between them were gone and their hearts had melted.

What followed changed the whole history of modern missions. That village of fewer than three hundred people began a round-the-clock relay of prayer, one shift handing on to the next, that continued for more than a hundred years. Out of that furnace of prayer went missionaries, wave after wave of them, to the West Indies, Greenland, Africa and South America. Years later an English clergyman named John Wesley (1703–1791) was caught in a storm at sea. He watched the Moravian believers on board singing hymns calmly while the waves crashed around them, and his heart was shaken. Not long afterwards, in Aldersgate Street in London, he felt his heart “strangely warmed”, and from there he set the whole Methodist movement in England ablaze.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it?

One man’s humbling brought a community into unity; one community’s unity brought a prayer meeting that lasted a hundred years; and one prayer meeting changed the destiny of several continents.

That is what today’s lesson is about: the three tiers of revival. Personal revival, revival of the church, revival of the Kingdom.

These three are not three parallel lines, nor three options from which you may pick one. They are three stretches of a single road, three rings rippling outward from one well of living water. Personal revival is for the sake of the church’s revival; the church’s revival is for the sake of the Kingdom’s revival; and the revival of the Kingdom is the very heart of Jesus Christ.

Let me put today’s conclusion up front: revival waits for no one, and it does not run on feelings. What it waits for is a people who are willing, day by day, to choose obedience, unity and wholehearted giving. And all of it begins with the choice you and I make right now.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Moment the Trumpet Sounds
sections.html: Before we open the three key points, let’s first stand where our theme verse originally stood. A verse gives off its own true light only when we return it to its context.

sections.heading: 1. Author, Date and Readers
sections.html:
The author of Revelation is the apostle John. Three times in the book he calls himself John (Revelation 1:1, 1:4, 22:8); he is the disciple whom the Lord Jesus loved. According to the consistent witness of church history, the book was written around AD 95, towards the end of the reign of the Roman emperor Domitian (who ruled AD 81–96). At the time John had been banished to the island of Patmos for preaching.

He puts it like this himself: “I John, your brother and partner with you in the oppression, Kingdom, and perseverance in Christ Jesus, was on the isle that is called Patmos because of God’s Word and the testimony of Jesus Christ.” (Revelation 1:9)

Notice the three words in that sentence: oppression, Kingdom, perseverance. Put those three together and you have the skeleton of Revelation. Believers are in tribulation now, they will enter the Kingdom in the future, and what they need in the meantime is perseverance.

The letter was addressed to seven churches in Asia Minor. These were not prosperous, triumphant churches. The church in Ephesus had left its first love; the church in Smyrna was in tribulation and poverty; the church in Pergamum lived where Satan’s throne is; the church in Thyatira had been infiltrated by false teaching; the church in Sardis had a name for being alive but was dead; the church in Laodicea was lukewarm. Only the church in Philadelphia received no rebuke from the Lord.

In other words, Revelation is not a victory song written for winners; it is a shot of courage for the weary.

sections.heading: 2. The Seventh Trumpet: From Contest to Belonging
sections.html:
Revelation 11:15 stands in the middle of the three series of visions — the seven seals, the seven trumpets and the seven bowls. The seventh angel’s trumpet is the last of the seven trumpets and the turning point of the whole book. As soon as it sounds, loud voices in heaven proclaim that the kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ.

One word here is worth stopping for. “The kingdom of the world” is, in the original Greek, the singular form of βασιλεία (basileia), meaning “kingship, royal rule”. It is not talking about territory on a map; it is talking about to whom sovereignty belongs. So what this verse really proclaims is this: the rule over this world has now changed hands.

Notice the tense of the verb. “Has become” is an aorist in the original, carrying the tone of something already settled. John is not saying “one day it will become”; he is saying that in God’s eternal plan this is already decided. Heaven proclaims it first; then it comes to pass on earth.

Brothers and sisters, this is the foundation for all our talk of revival. Revival is not us straining to snatch the world back. Revival is our response to the proclamation heaven has already made — letting that kingship, already accomplished, be acknowledged and displayed step by step in my life, in our church and in this land.

sections.heading: 3. What the Word “Revival” Originally Means
sections.html:
When the Bible speaks of revival, the Hebrew verb it often uses is חָיָה (chayah), whose basic meaning is “to live”. Its causative form means “to make alive again”. So the psalmist prays:

“Won’t you revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?” (Psalm 85:6)

“Revive” is chayah. The essence of revival is not dressing up something dead so it looks a little nicer; it is putting breath back into what was dead.

The prophet Habakkuk asked the same thing: “Yahweh, I have heard of your fame. I stand in awe of your deeds, Yahweh. Renew your work in the middle of the years. In the middle of the years make it known. In wrath, you remember mercy.” (Habakkuk 3:2)

In the New Testament, Peter, preaching in Solomon’s Porch, used another word. He said: “whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration of all things, which God spoke long ago by the mouth of his holy prophets.” (Acts 3:21) The Greek for “restoration of all things” is ἀποκατάστασις (apokatastasis), meaning “restoration to the state something was always meant to be in”.

Put those two words together and revival becomes clear: revival is making the dead live again, setting the crooked straight, bringing everything back to God’s original intention in creation.

So revival is not an emotional high, nor the stirring of a single special conference. Revival is God’s life moving again; it is God’s order being established again.

And the order in which God does this is: first one person, then a group of people, and then the whole earth.

Brothers and sisters, let’s now look at it step by step.

sections.heading: 1. Personal Revival: Change That Begins with a Choice
sections.html:
1. Revival Starts with a Heart Set Alight Again

The lesson puts it plainly: personal revival is the starting point and the foundation of the end time revival.

The first thing God wants to do is not to hand us a plan or give us a set of methods, but to set alight again our love and zeal for Jesus, to awaken the heart that once burned for the Lord.

What the Lord Jesus said to the church in Ephesus is worth each of us hearing quietly once more this morning:

“But I have this against you, that you left your first love. Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works.” (Revelation 2:4-5)

Notice the Lord’s diagnosis. He did not say the church in Ephesus wasn’t doing enough. In fact the Lord praised them first: “I know your works, and your toil and perseverance” (Revelation 2:2). They had works, they had toil, they had perseverance, and they had the discernment to expose false teaching. And yet the Lord said: there is one thing.

One thing. Not ten — one.

You left your first love.

Brothers and sisters, what a sobering warning this is. A person can serve without a break while their love grows cold; a person can never miss a meeting while their heart is elsewhere; a person can expound a great deal of teaching and yet not have shed a single tear for the Lord in a very long time.

The Lord’s prescription has three parts: remember, repent, do the first works. Remembering is the reawakening of memory; repenting is the turning around of direction; doing the first works is the restarting of action.

All three parts of the prescription point to the same thing — coming back to Jesus.

The disciples of the early church were ordinary people. Peter was a fisherman, Matthew a tax collector, Simon a Zealot. They had no learning and no standing. When the council “saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus” (Acts 4:13).

Look at that line: they recognised that they had been with Jesus.

Their lives were turned completely upside down — no longer living for themselves, but willing to give themselves to the Lord without holding anything back — and there is only one explanation: they had met Jesus.

2. The Key to Personal Revival Is Choice

The lesson says: the key to personal revival lies in choice.

That sentence deserves a whole morning of reflection.

We often think of revival as something that “happens” — one day the Holy Spirit suddenly pours out, and suddenly I’m on fire. We would never deny the sovereignty of the Holy Spirit; the wind blows where it wills. But the Bible tells us just as clearly that God never forces anyone. He puts the choice in our hands.

At the end of his life Joshua gathered all Israel at Shechem and said to them:

“If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose today whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell; but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.” (Joshua 24:15)

“Choose today.”

Revival isn’t tomorrow’s business; it’s today’s. It isn’t “let’s wait until things get better”; it’s making the decision now.

And what is the content of that choice? The lesson says: leaving the self-centred system and returning to God’s system.

This is the very heart of the 321 vision. The problem of the old self can be summed up in one word — “self”. “Self” is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. Satan’s “I will” long ago was nothing other than putting himself in God’s place. From that moment on there have been two systems in the universe: one centred on self and one centred on God.

So personal revival, in the end, is a transfer of sovereignty. The lesson puts it beautifully: this is not merely a change of outward behaviour; it is a transfer of sovereignty that begins in the heart — no longer being king myself, but letting Jesus reign in my life.

Paul sums it up in one sentence:

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

“No longer I, but Christ.” That is selflessness.

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: selflessness is not having nothing. It is not wiping yourself out, not becoming a person with no thoughts and no feelings. Selflessness is “zero” — setting yourself back to zero so that God’s infinity can flow out through you. A zero on its own is nothing; but put it after a one and it becomes ten; add another zero and it becomes a hundred.

Selflessness is not becoming smaller; selflessness is entering into the infinite.

3. A Confirmation from Psychology: Habits and “If–Then Plans”

Psychology offers a fascinating piece of supporting evidence here.

In a study published in 2002 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the University of Southern California psychologist Wendy Wood and her colleagues found that around 43 per cent of what people do each day is habitual behaviour, repeated in the same settings.

In other words, we think we are “deciding” all day long, but nearly half the time we are simply “replaying”.

That is why so many people pray year after year, “Lord, revive me,” and never change. We are asking for a feeling, but the track of a life is laid by choices; without new choices, there is only the old replay.

So how do we break the replay?

In a paper published in 1999 in American Psychologist, the New York University psychologist Peter Gollwitzer put forward a concept called “implementation intentions” — that is, “if … then …” plans. He found that a vague goal (“I’m going to exercise more”) often comes to nothing; but write it as a specific trigger (“If my alarm goes off at seven in the morning, then I put on my shoes and go out”), and the rate of success rises markedly.

Brothers and sisters, spiritual training works the same way.

Don’t just say, “I want to love the Lord more.” Say: “If I wake up in the morning, then my first words will be: Lord, today it is not about what I want; may your will be done.”

Don’t just say, “I want to obey the Holy Spirit.” Say: “If I feel a prick of conviction in my heart, then I will stop at once and go no further.”

Only specific choices become a new track.

Of course, psychology is only a helper. What truly changes people is not technique; it is the Holy Spirit. Zechariah said it long ago: “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.” (Zechariah 4:6) Methods help us set our hearts in the right place; the Holy Spirit is the one who lights the fire.

4. Applying the 321 Vision: Fivefold Change Begins with Mindset

The 321 vision says that human change is fivefold: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry.

Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry.

Notice that the starting point is mindset, not ministry. Many people are in a hurry to “do something” without first letting their mindset be turned around. The result is new ministry done with an old mindset, God’s work done in the way of “self” — and the more we do, the more tired and empty we become.

Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

“Transformed by the renewing of your mind”: the Greek for “renewing” is ἀνακαίνωσις (anakainōsis), a renewal of the very nature of a thing, not a surface renovation. And “conformed” and “transformed” are two quite different words in the original: the first speaks of imitating an outward shape; the second speaks of a change of substance from the inside out — and it is the very word used when the Lord Jesus was transfigured on the mountain (Matthew 17:2).

Brothers and sisters, what God wants is not for us to look like Christians on the outside; what God wants is for us to be truly changed inside into the likeness of Christ.

And the shift in perspective runs in four directions: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from a temporary perspective to an eternal one, and from a worldly perspective to a godly one.

Look at something from far enough away and its weight changes. The person who made you angry this morning, seen in the light of eternity, is your “2”; the thing that is making you anxious today, seen from heaven, is no more than a tool in the Lord’s hand.

5. The Lesson’s Practices for Daily Living (Personal)

The lesson has prepared three practices for us. Let’s take them one at a time.

First, every morning, hand over your sovereignty again in prayer: “Lord, today it is not about what I want; may your will be done.”

This is the road the Lord Jesus himself walked. In Gethsemane he said: “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” (Matthew 26:39) Revival never begins with getting; it begins with handing over.

Second, pay deliberate attention to the promptings of the Holy Spirit and learn to obey in small things. A little more patience with your family; choosing honesty at work.

Why small things? Because the Lord said: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). The voice of the Holy Spirit is usually quiet, and it shows up in small things. A person who ignores the Holy Spirit in small things will not hear him in big things either.

Third, examine yourself once a week: “Where did I indulge myself this week? In what things did I let Jesus be King?”

This is what 321 calls Evaluation. Without evaluation, practice is only motion; with evaluation, practice becomes life.

The lesson ends by saying: as more and more believers begin to make choices like these, personal revival will spread step by step and prepare the way for the revival of the church.

One candle lights another and grows no dimmer for it. That is the arithmetic of revival.

sections.heading: 2. Revival of the Church: The Power of Multiplication in Unity
sections.html:
1. Revival Is Not Numbers; It Is a Body Joined Together

The lesson says: the end time revival is not the revival of a few individuals; it is the renewal and transformation of the whole church.

Notice this sentence in the lesson: if a church truly experiences revival, it is not merely an increase in numbers; it is relationships full of love and sincerity, full of the Lord’s presence and the power of witness.

That sentence puts the centre of gravity of revival back where it belongs. Numbers will grow — that is the fruit; relationships are renewed — that is the root.

Acts chapter 2 gives us a complete picture. On the day of Pentecost Peter stood up and preached, and Scripture records:

“Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls.” (Acts 2:41)

This is how the biblical record puts it: on the day of Pentecost about three thousand were added (Acts 2:41); later “many of those who heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to be about five thousand” (Acts 4:4); and “the Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved” (Acts 2:47).

Added day by day — that is God’s work, not human ability. On that point the lesson is entirely right.

But notice that before the growth in numbers, Scripture first records the way they lived:

“They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer.” (Acts 2:42)

“Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart, praising God, and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.” (Acts 2:46-47)

First came “with one accord”; then came “added day by day”. First relationships, then growth.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the order 321 speaks of: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

2. What the Lord Prayed for the Church Is Unity

On the night before he went to the cross, the Lord Jesus prayed for believers of every generation:

“that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21)

Look at the structure of this prayer. The standard of unity is the unity of the Father and the Son; the purpose of unity is that the world may believe.

In other words, unity itself is the most powerful witness to the gospel. The world may not be able to read our theology, but it can read our relationships.

Paul describes it with the picture of a body:

“but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ, from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love.” (Ephesians 4:15-16)

“Fitted and knit together”, “every joint supplies”, “the working … of each individual part”, and then — “makes the body increase”.

Brothers and sisters, do you see the cause and effect? Growth is the result of being joined together. If a body has dislocated joints and torn ligaments, however much you feed it, it will not grow well.

The psalm says: “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1) And the psalm ends: “for there Yahweh gives the blessing, even life forever more.” (Psalm 133:3)

The blessing God has ordained is found “there” — in the place where brothers live together in unity. The place of unity is the channel of blessing.

3. The Mark of Revival Is Multiplication, Not Division

The lesson makes a vital statement: one important mark of the church’s revival is “multiplication”, but this multiplication is not division; it is increase within unity.

What is the difference between the two?

Division is splitting apart because relationships have broken; multiplication is expanding because life is overflowing. After a division, both sides are wounded; after a multiplication, both sides grow.

The root of division, as 321 makes clear, is pride. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place. Pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win.

And what does Paul say?

“doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others. Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 2:3-5)

“Each counting others better than himself” — that is the secret of unity, and it is the practice of humility.

And true multiplication looks like this:

“The word of God increased and the number of the disciples greatly multiplied in Jerusalem. A great company of the priests were obedient to the faith.” (Acts 6:7)

What’s striking is that the verses just before this one record the church handling a conflict — the Greek-speaking Jews complained against the Hebrews because their widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution. The apostles neither suppressed the matter nor let it tear the church apart. Instead they appointed seven deacons, and the problem became the occasion for a new office to be born.

A conflict handled rightly becomes a doorway to multiplication.

Paul handed Timothy the method of multiplication: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2)

There are four generations in that one verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. The multiplication of life depends not on events but on people bringing people along.

4. Supporting Evidence from Science and Research: The Power of Relationships

The Harvard Study of Adult Development began in 1938 and has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years, making it one of the longest-running longitudinal studies ever conducted. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, has explained its clearest conclusion many times in public: good relationships do more than wealth or fame to keep people healthy and happy, and help them live longer.

When God made man he said: “It is not good for the man to be alone” (Genesis 2:18). Eighty years of scientific research have simply written a footnote to that ancient sentence.

Another example comes from the workplace. Between 2012 and 2015 Google ran “Project Aristotle”, studying well over a hundred teams within the company to discover what makes a team effective. It found that the most important factor was not how clever the members were or how many degrees they held, but the team’s “psychological safety” — a concept put forward in 1999 by Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School, meaning that members dare to admit mistakes and voice disagreement without fear of being humiliated.

Brothers and sisters, if everyone in a church has to keep up appearances and no one dares to admit weakness, that is not holiness; that is fear. A truly revived church is a place where people dare to speak the truth and dare to shed tears.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: 235 Relationships and the 920 Practice

The lesson’s three practices fit neatly with two of 321’s frameworks for practice.

The first practice: build a culture of spiritual family — not just coming to meetings, but building genuine relationships with brothers and sisters, loving and supporting one another.

This is the first step of “235 relationships”. Find someone who will pursue selflessness together with you, to be your “2” — your spiritual companion. Two people, not for the sake of pouring out complaints, but to remind one another, pray for one another and build one another up.

The second practice: learn to be a disciple and to make disciples — take the initiative to care for and walk alongside a spiritual companion, building one another up and growing together.

This is the second step of “235” — establishing your “3”: spiritual parents and spiritual children. With spiritual parents we won’t go astray; with spiritual children we won’t stagnate. Go further still and you come to the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12).

The third practice: be of one heart with the church’s leaders — not criticising or judging, but praying for them, supporting them, and taking up together God’s vision for the church.

This one is the hardest, yet the most crucial. Because criticism is pride’s most convenient outlet. A word of criticism costs nothing, yet it can make us look clever.

This is where the 920 practice comes in: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. Facing that person, we practise living out the selfless life (0) and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions —

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22-23)

Brothers and sisters, next time you feel like criticising someone, put that person in the place of your “2”, and ask yourself: which fruit do I need to bring out right now?

The lesson’s conclusion is beautifully put: the church’s revival is not a flurry of activities; it is the joining together of a body.
