prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

You have said that if your people, who are called by your name, will humble themselves, pray, seek your face, and turn from their wicked ways, you will hear from heaven, forgive our sin and heal our land. Lord, today we stand on this promise.
Forgive us for our passivity. We have waited too long without breaking up the fallow ground; we have sought your hand far too much, and sought your face far too little.
Lord, I humble myself before you. I hand my throne back to you. From this morning on, I am not the one in charge; you are King.
Holy Spirit, help me, before every conflict and every decision, first to be still and ask you, “Jesus, what do you want me to do?”
Give me a heart that longs for you, willing to stop each week and set apart time to seek you alone. Speak to me in the stillness, and let me hear your still small voice.

Lord, revive me, so that through me you can revive my family, my small group, my church and my city.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.

blocks.x: Subtitle: Three small practices that walk God’s promise into everyday life

A man stands on a railway platform, ticket in hand, and waits for three hours. The train never comes. A station attendant walks past, glances at his ticket and says, “Sir, this train leaves from the platform on the other side.”
It wasn’t that he had no ticket. It wasn’t that he didn’t want to get on. He was simply standing in the wrong place.

That is so often how we approach revival. We have the promises, we have the longing, and we pray — yet one year waits out the next, and we always feel the train still hasn’t pulled into the station. Perhaps the problem isn’t on God’s side.
Hidden in God’s promise are four things for us to do

“If my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” (2 Chronicles 7:14)

This verse is often quoted, but often only half read. The second half holds God’s three promises: to hear, to forgive, to heal. But the first half holds our four things: to humble ourselves, to pray, to seek his face, and to turn from our wicked ways.

Its setting is even more striking. These words come straight after verse 13, which speaks of the sky shut up with no rain, locusts devouring the land, and pestilence among the people. God did not say this when all was calm; it is the road home he left for his people after foretelling disaster.
Hosea speaks of the same order: “Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.” (Hosea 10:12)

First the ground is broken up; then the rain comes. The rain is God’s gift; no human being can make a single drop of rain. But the fallow ground is ours to break up. God will not pick up the hoe for us.

Revival is God’s work, and our responsibility is to prepare. It’s like electricity: the power station supplies it, and you can’t make it yourself; but the wiring in your home has to be connected and the switch turned on.
Three small practices that give revival a rhythm

Revival doesn’t happen only in a meeting. The warmth of a good meeting often doesn’t survive the car park. True revival is a different kind of life at the dinner table, at your desk in the office, in the conversations between husband and wife. What we need is not more stirring moments, but a rhythm we can repeat.

First, active obedience every day. The first thing you do when you wake up is not check your phone, but close your eyes and say to the Lord, “Lord Jesus, today I am not the one in charge; you are King.” Thirty seconds is enough. Then, before every conflict or decision, silently ask, “Jesus, what do you want me to do?” Justifying yourself the moment you are misunderstood is the self-centred life speaking; taking a step back to ask the Lord first is selflessness breathing.

Second, fasting and prayer every week. Choose one day a week — or even just one meal — and set that time apart as holy. Fasting is not going hungry in exchange for God’s yes, nor is it harsh self-punishment. “Tear your heart, and not your garments.” (Joel 2:13) Fasting doesn’t create problems; it simply turns the volume down so that you can hear the voice that was there all along. You can pray for three things: repentance for the coldness and pride in your own heart, the unity and purity of the church, and the expansion of the Kingdom and the Lord’s return.

Third, choosing to deny yourself every week. Choose one person — your spouse, your child, a co-worker, a friend — and express the love of Christ to them in a concrete way: an apology, a word of encouragement, a meal, a hug. These acts may look ordinary, but they are the most powerful tools for tearing down the enemy’s strongholds. Because love makes us one, and oneness brings the Lord glory.

Psychological research reminds us to be patient. A 2010 study by Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London found that it takes on average about sixty-six days for a new habit to become automatic, and that missing the occasional day does not undermine the forming of the habit. If you miss a day, just pick it up again the next.
It is now, and it is you

In 1727, a small band of believers in Herrnhut in Germany first confessed their sins and were reconciled to one another, then began keeping watch in prayer in shifts — and that prayer went on for more than a hundred years. In 1857, the New York businessman Jeremiah Lanphier held a lunchtime prayer meeting; on the first day only six people came, but the wave later spread across the whole of America. God never despises how small your starting point is. He only asks whether you are willing to be the first to kneel down.

Revival will not suddenly drop out of the sky; it begins little by little in your life and mine. This is God’s moment — not some time in the future, and not waiting for someone else. It is now, and it is you.
Not waiting for the pastor to warm up first, not waiting for the small-group leader to change first, not waiting for your spouse to apologise first. It’s you.

May we rise up, no longer looking on, no longer putting it off, but with one choice, one prayer and one action, press on into the great revival God has already prepared for us. Let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.
Reflection
Of the four things — humbling yourself, praying, seeking his face and turning from wicked ways — which is currently your weakest? This week, what is the first concrete step you will take about it?

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we’re reading Lesson 10 together, “No More Waiting — It’s Time to Press On into Revival”. Our theme verse is 2 Chronicles 7:14: “If my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” In this one verse there are four things for us to do, and three promises from God.

Let me paint a picture first. A man is standing on a railway platform, ticket in hand. He waits three hours, and the train never comes. A station attendant says, “Sir, this train leaves from the other side.” It wasn’t that he had no ticket; he was simply standing in the wrong place. Brothers and sisters, isn’t that how we approach revival? The lesson puts it clearly: it is not because God is unwilling, but because on our side we have not yet aligned ourselves with his heart. Hosea 10:12 says, “Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes.” Notice the order: first the ground is broken up, then the rain comes. The rain is God’s gift; the fallow ground is ours to break up. Revival is not waited for; it is walked out.

Who was this verse spoken to? Chronicles was written after the return from exile, for a remnant who had just come back to Jerusalem. The walls were broken, the temple was humble, and their hearts were grey. More important still is the context: in chapter 7, verse 13, God first speaks of the sky shut up with no rain, locusts devouring the land and pestilence among the people, and only in verse 14 does he give the way out. This is not a nice-sounding slogan. It is the road home God left for his people in their darkest hour.

The first point: revival is God’s work, and we are responsible to prepare. Zechariah 4:6 says, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.” But God also clearly sets out our responsibility: to humble ourselves, to pray, to seek his face, and to turn from our wicked ways. It’s like electricity. The power station supplies it, and you can’t make it yourself; but the wiring in your home has to be connected and the switch turned on. In 1727, the believers at Herrnhut in Germany first confessed their sins and were reconciled, and then the Holy Spirit was poured out; twenty-four brothers and twenty-four sisters kept up a relay of prayer for more than a hundred years. In 1857, the New York businessman Jeremiah Lanphier held a lunchtime prayer meeting; on the first day only six people came, yet it spread across the whole of America. God never despises how small your starting point is. He only asks whether you are willing to be the first to kneel down.

The second point: only God’s system can enter into God’s revival. The lesson says that what this age needs is not more programmes and events, but more lives willing to let Jesus be King. Romans 12:2 says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” In the original, “conformed” speaks of an outward shell, while “transformed” speaks of essential form — the very word we use for a caterpillar becoming a butterfly. Brothers and sisters, can you hear the difference? The world wants you to change your shell; God wants to change your life. In the chrysalis, most of a caterpillar’s tissue is broken down and then rebuilt into a butterfly. It isn’t a caterpillar with wings fitted on; it is a new creation.

The third point, and the first practice: active obedience every day — let Jesus be King. The lesson says that the first thing you do when you wake up is not check your phone or plan your schedule, but close your eyes and say to the Lord, “Lord Jesus, today I am not the one in charge; you are King.” Psalm 5:3 says, “In the morning I will lay my requests before you.” The Lord Jesus himself rose before dawn to pray. Let me ask you: when you’re misunderstood at work, do you justify yourself straight away, or do you first take a step back and ask, “Lord, how do you want me to respond?” Justifying yourself straight away is the self-centred life; asking the Lord first is selflessness. How to practise: every morning pray about sovereignty, and before every conflict or decision silently ask the Lord first.

The second practice: fasting and prayer every week, fixing our hearts on God. The lesson says to choose one day a week to fast — one meal or the whole day — and set that day apart as holy; not only stopping eating and drinking, but stopping the voices of the world, so that we can hear the voice of God. Joel 2:13 says, “Tear your heart, and not your garments.” If fasting doesn’t bring a broken heart, it’s nothing more than a diet. The lesson says to pray for three things while fasting: repentance for our own coldness and pride, the unity and purity of the church, and the expansion of the Kingdom and the Lord’s return. That is exactly first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

The third practice: choosing to deny ourselves every week, living out selflessness. The lesson says that revival is not only in the prayer meeting; even more, it is lived out in our relationships with one another. This week, choose one person and express the love of Christ to them in a concrete way: an apology, a word of encouragement, a meal, a hug. In the original, “deny himself” means “disown oneself”. Peter disowned the Lord, but disciples are called to disown themselves. Paul says, “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). These acts may look ordinary, but they are the most powerful tools for tearing down the enemy’s strongholds — because love makes us one, and oneness brings the Lord glory.

Brothers and sisters, these three practices are not three scattered good deeds, but one clear road. 321 says change is fivefold: a change of mindset — revival is walked out; a change of life — letting Jesus be King; a change of daily living — obeying every day and fasting every week; a change of relationships — denying ourselves every week; a change of ministry — the Kingdom expanding naturally. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

So what do we do from today? Three actions: pray about sovereignty every morning; fast one day or one meal each week and be still to hear God speak; and each week take the initiative to care for and bless one person. And walk it through with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. The principle of Correction is to lower the threshold, not the standard. Give yourself three months; if you miss a day, pick it up again the next. And finally, Multiplication — find a companion to walk with, and check in with each other once a week.

This is how the lesson closes: dear brothers and sisters, revival will not suddenly drop out of the sky; it begins little by little in your life and mine. Today, if we are willing to begin to obey, to fast and seek, to choose to deny ourselves and live out selflessness, the Spirit of God will move among us. This is God’s moment — not some time in the future, and not waiting for someone else. It is now, and it is you. Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to those two words: it’s you. Not waiting for the pastor to warm up first, not waiting for your spouse to apologise first. It’s you.

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, you have said that if we humble ourselves, pray, seek your face and turn from our wicked ways, you will hear, forgive and heal. Forgive us for our passivity; we have sought your hand far too much and sought your face far too little. Lord, I humble myself before you. I hand my throne back to you. From this morning on, I am not the one in charge; you are King. Revive me, so that through me you can revive my family and my church. Let your Kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless you; let Jesus be King every day this week.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we’re reading Lesson 10 together, “No More Waiting — It’s Time to Press On into Revival”. Our theme verse is 2 Chronicles 7:14: “If my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” Please remember the structure of this verse: the first half is our four things, and the second half is God’s three promises.

Let me paint a picture first. A man is standing on a railway platform, gripping his ticket tightly. He waits an hour, and no train comes; he waits two hours, and still no train. A station attendant walks past, glances at his ticket and says, “Sir, this train leaves from the platform on the other side.” Brothers and sisters, it wasn’t that he had no ticket, and it wasn’t that he didn’t want to get on. He was simply standing in the wrong place. I want to ask you honestly: isn’t that how we approach revival? We hold the promises, we long for it in our hearts, we pray for it with our lips — and yet one year waits out the next, one conference waits out the next.

Right at the start, the lesson says something of real weight: if we have not yet seen revival fully realised, it is not because God is unwilling, but because on our side we have not yet fully aligned ourselves with his heart. Brothers and sisters, that sentence is like a key. God’s fire has long been ready; it is only that the altar has not been repaired. God’s rain has long filled the sky; it is only that the field has not been broken up. Hosea 10:12 says, “Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.” Notice the order: first the ground is broken up, then the rain comes. The rain is God’s gift; no human being can make a single drop. But the fallow ground is ours to break up. So revival is not waited for; it is walked out.

Let’s look at the background first. Chronicles was written after the return from exile, around the fifth century BC, for a remnant who had just come back to Jerusalem. The walls were broken, the temple was humble, and when the older people saw the foundation of the second temple laid, they actually wept aloud. The question in their hearts was: will God’s glory ever return? More important still is the context. In chapter 7, verse 13, God first says: if I shut up the sky so that there is no rain, or command the locust to devour the land, or send pestilence among my people. First the disaster; only in verse 14 the way out. Brothers and sisters, this is not a nice-sounding slogan. It is the road home God left for his people in their darkest hour.

The first point: revival is God’s work. The lesson puts it clearly: revival is not a human plan, nor something human effort can force into being. We have to stand firmly on this first; otherwise all our practices will become just another form of relying on ourselves. Zechariah 4:6 says, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.” Habakkuk prayed, “Renew your work in the middle of the years” (Habakkuk 3:2). Notice — revive “your” work, not ours.

So what is our responsibility? God hasn’t left us to stand by with folded arms. He sets out four things: humble ourselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from wicked ways. There’s an important distinction here: to seek his “hand” is to want what he gives; to seek his “face” is to want him. It’s like electricity. The power station supplies it, and you can’t make it yourself; but the wiring in your home has to be connected and the switch turned on. In 1727, the believers at Herrnhut in Germany first confessed their sins and were reconciled; on 13 August the Holy Spirit was poured out, and soon twenty-four brothers and twenty-four sisters began keeping watch in shifts — a prayer that lasted more than a hundred years. In 1857, the New York businessman Jeremiah Lanphier held a lunchtime prayer meeting; on the first day only six people came, but the wave later spread across the whole of America. God never despises how small your starting point is. He only asks whether you are willing to be the first to kneel down.

The second point: only God’s system can enter into God’s revival. The lesson says that true revival does not just happen in church meetings; it begins in the life of each individual. What this age needs is not more programmes and events, but more lives willing to let Jesus be King. Brothers and sisters, the warmth of a good meeting often doesn’t survive the car park. True revival is a different kind of life at your dinner table, at your desk in the office, in the conversations between husband and wife.

Paul says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2). In the original, the root of “conformed” is an outward pattern, like changing your clothes or your phone case; the root of “transformed” is essential form — the very word we use for a caterpillar becoming a butterfly. Brothers and sisters, the world wants you to change your shell; God wants to change your life. After a caterpillar forms its chrysalis, most of its tissue is broken down, and then clusters of cells called imaginal discs rebuild it into a butterfly. It is not a caterpillar with wings bolted on; it is a new creation. This is moving from the self-centred old self into the selfless new self; it is also the shift of perspective — from man’s to God’s, from the temporal to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

Next come the three practices. The first: active obedience every day — let Jesus be King. The lesson says that the first thing you do when you wake up is not check your phone or plan your schedule, but close your eyes and say to the Lord, “Lord Jesus, today I am not the one in charge; you are King.” Brothers and sisters, when you woke up this morning, what was the first thing you did? For many people, the answer is: reach for the phone. Our day has very often been set for us by other people before we have said a single word to God. Psalm 5:3 says, “In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.” The Lord Jesus himself rose before dawn and went out to a deserted place to pray. If even the Son of God did that, what makes us think we can do without it?

The lesson gives an example: when you are misunderstood at work, do you immediately justify yourself, or do you first take a step back and ask, “Lord, how do you want me to respond?” Brothers and sisters, the difference of that one second decides between two completely different lives. Justifying yourself straight away is the self-centred life speaking; asking the Lord first is selflessness breathing. There’s a vivid picture: many people have invited Jesus into the car, but they make him sit in the back seat, and having asked his opinion they go on driving themselves. Letting Jesus be King means he is in the driver’s seat and you don’t touch the steering wheel. Samuel said, “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22). We can serve very busily and yet never let Jesus be King all day long.

Why “every day”? Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). Notice that word: daily. The cross is not a piece of luggage you carry once and are done with. Psychology gives us a practical reminder too: in a study published in 2010, Phillippa Lally of University College London and her colleagues found that it took on average about sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit; the same study also found that missing the occasional day did not significantly undermine the forming of the habit. So don’t expect results after three days, and don’t give up because you missed one day. How to practise: every morning pray about sovereignty, and before every conflict or decision silently ask the Lord first.

The second practice: fasting and prayer every week, fixing our hearts on God. The lesson says to choose one day a week to fast — one meal or the whole day — and set that day apart as holy; not only stopping eating and drinking, but stopping the voices of the world, so that we can hear the voice of God. Here is an apt illustration. The Japanese scientist Yoshinori Ohsumi was awarded the 2016 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for explaining the mechanisms of cellular autophagy: when cells are short of nutrients, they break down and recycle old and damaged components. I am not saying fasting can save anyone; salvation is by grace alone, through faith. What I am saying is that the body God made is itself speaking a language: when the supply from outside is paused, the clean-up inside begins.

Fasting is most easily misunderstood in two ways: as going hungry in exchange for God’s yes, or as harsh self-punishment. Scripture teaches neither. Joel 2:13 says, “Tear your heart, and not your garments.” In the ancient Near East, tearing your clothes was the sign of grief; God says, “I don’t want that garment; I want your heart.” Brothers and sisters, if fasting doesn’t bring a broken heart, it’s nothing more than a diet. And the Lord Jesus says, “But you, when you fast, anoint your head, and wash your face; so that you are not seen by men to be fasting, but by your Father who is in secret” (Matthew 6:17-18). Notice that the Lord says “when you fast”, not “if you fast”.

The lesson tells us to pray for three things while we fast. First, repent of the coldness and pride in our own hearts — the first stop of revival is always our own heart. Second, pray for the unity and purity of the church; the Lord Jesus’ farewell prayer was “that they may all be one” (John 17:21). Third, pray for the expansion of the Kingdom and the preparation for the Lord’s return; the Lord taught us to pray, “Let your Kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10). Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? This is exactly first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Acts chapter 13 records that the first commissioning for cross-cultural mission in history was issued in the middle of a time of fasting and prayer. How to practise: choose one day each week to fast at least one meal, spend quiet time alone, and write down the key things the Holy Spirit brings to mind. If you have particular health conditions, please consult your doctor first.

The third practice: choosing to deny ourselves every week, living out selflessness. The lesson says that revival is not only in the prayer meeting; even more, it is lived out in our relationships with one another. The mistake we most easily make is to lock revival up inside our meetings; a person can weep buckets in a prayer meeting and then go home and be unable to say a simple “I’m sorry”. The lesson says: choose one person — your spouse, your child, a co-worker, an acquaintance — and express the love of Christ to them in a concrete way: an apology, a word of encouragement, a meal, a hug. In the original, “deny himself” literally means “disown oneself”, and it shares its root with Peter’s “denying the Lord”. Peter disowned the Lord, but disciples are called to disown themselves. Paul says, “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

The lesson offers a spiritual insight: these acts may look ordinary, but they are the most powerful tools for tearing down the enemy’s strongholds, because love makes us one, and oneness brings the Lord glory. Psalm 133 says, “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” And it ends, “for there Yahweh gives the blessing.” Look at that one word: “there”. Brothers and sisters, the blessing was ordained long ago; it is just that it comes down on the place where people live together in unity. If you are not there, it is not that there is no blessing; it is that you are not at the delivery address. A 2008 study by Dunn, Aknin and Norton in the journal Science also found that people who spent money on others were happier than those who spent it on themselves. This is exactly what 321 says: people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Brothers and sisters, let me say the three practices once more. First, every morning pray about sovereignty, and before every conflict or decision ask the Lord first, “Jesus, what do you want me to do?” Second, choose one day each week to fast at least one meal, spend quiet time alone, and write down the Holy Spirit’s promptings. Third, each week take the initiative to care for one person, bless them with practical action, and name them in prayer. The lesson puts it well: not waiting until we feel moved before we act, but having concrete practices and disciplines even in the most ordinary days.

Now let’s use the eight stages of changing our mindset to plant these three practices into our daily living. Information: copy the three practices onto a card, and memorise 2 Chronicles 7:14. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to speak — Lord, where am I still not aligned with you? Conviction: write down the resistance in your heart, with a verse beside each objection. Implementation: start today; don’t wait for next Monday. Evaluation: every Sunday evening ask yourself on how many days this week you really gave up the throne. Correction: lower the threshold, not the standard. Repetition: give yourself three months; if you miss a day, pick it up again the next. Multiplication: find a companion to walk with, and check in with each other every week.

Let’s set the whole lesson back into the picture of 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. The fivefold change: a change of mindset — revival is walked out; a change of life — from self-centred to selfless; a change of daily living — obeying every day and fasting every week; a change of relationships — denying ourselves every week; a change of ministry — the Kingdom expanding naturally. So: life first, then relationships, then ministry. James says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). Pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility inspires humility and both sides win. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

As for the lesson’s closing words, I want to read them to you almost word for word. Dear brothers and sisters, revival will not suddenly drop out of the sky; it begins little by little in your life and mine. Today, if we are willing to begin to obey, to fast and seek, to choose to deny ourselves and live out selflessness, the Spirit of God will move among us. This is God’s moment — not some time in the future, and not waiting for someone else. It is now, and it is you. Listen carefully to those two words: it’s you. Not waiting for the pastor to warm up first, not waiting for your spouse to apologise first. It’s you. When Moses saw the bush burning and yet not consumed, he said, “I will go now, and see this great sight” (Exodus 3:3). If he had not turned aside, God would not have called to him from the bush. God’s fire is already there. The question is whether you will turn aside.

Let’s bow our heads and pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, you have said that if we humble ourselves, pray, seek your face and turn from our wicked ways, you will hear, forgive and heal. Lord, today we stand on this promise. Forgive us for our passivity; we have sought your hand far too much and sought your face far too little. Lord, I humble myself before you. I hand my throne back to you. From this morning on, I am not the one in charge; you are King. Holy Spirit, help me, before every decision, first to be still and ask you: Jesus, what do you want me to do? Pour your love into my heart, so that this week I can step out towards that one person. Revive me, so that through me you can revive my family, my small group and my church. Let your Kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, may the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine on you. This week, let Jesus be King every day.
